<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-valgrind" rel="next">Using Valgrind</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Checking-memory-access" rel="up">Checking memory access</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.3.1 Using `gctorture` <a href="#Using-gctorture-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-gctorture" class="index-entry-id"></span>

We can help to detect memory problems in R objects earlier by running garbage collection as often as possible. This is achieved by `gctorture(TRUE)`, which as described on its help page

> Provokes garbage collection on (nearly) every memory allocation. Intended to ferret out memory protection bugs. Also makes R run *very* slowly, unfortunately.

The reference to ‘memory protection’ is to missing C-level calls to `PROTECT`/`UNPROTECT` (see <a href="#Garbage-Collection" class="pxref">Handling the effects of garbage collection</a>) which if missing allow R objects to be garbage-collected when they are still in use. But it can also help with other memory-related errors.

Normally running under `gctorture(TRUE)` will just produce a crash earlier in the R program, hopefully close to the actual cause. See the next section for how to decipher such crashes.

It is possible to run all the examples, tests and vignettes covered by `R CMD check` under `gctorture(TRUE)` by using the option `--use-gct`.

The function `gctorture2` provides more refined control over the <span class="abbr abbr">GC</span> torture process. Its arguments `step`, `wait` and `inhibit_release` are documented on its help page. Environment variables can also be used at the start of the R session to turn on <span class="abbr abbr">GC</span> torture: `R_GCTORTURE` corresponds to the `step` argument to `gctorture2`, `R_GCTORTURE_WAIT` to `wait`, and `R_GCTORTURE_INHIBIT_RELEASE` to `inhibit_release`.

If R is configured with `--enable-strict-barrier` then a variety of tests for the integrity of the write barrier are enabled. In addition tests to help detect protect issues are enabled:

- All <span class="abbr abbr">GC</span>s are full <span class="abbr abbr">GC</span>s.
- New nodes in small node pages are marked as `NEWSXP` on creation.
- After a <span class="abbr abbr">GC</span> all free nodes that are not of type `NEWSXP` are marked as type `FREESXP` and their previous type is recorded.
- Most calls to accessor functions check their `SEXP` inputs and `SEXP` outputs and signal an error if a `FREESXP` is found. The address of the node and the old type are included in the error message.

`R CMD check --use-gct` can be set to use `gctorture2(``n``)` rather than `gctorture(TRUE)` by setting environment variable `_R_CHECK_GCT_N_` to a positive integer value to be used as `n`.

Used with a debugger and with `gctorture` or `gctorture2` this mechanism can be helpful in isolating memory protect problems.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Using-valgrind" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-Address-Sanitizer" rel="next">Using the Address Sanitizer</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-gctorture" rel="prev">Using <code class="code">gctorture</code></a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Checking-memory-access" rel="up">Checking memory access</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.3.2 Using Valgrind <a href="#Using-Valgrind" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

If you have access to Linux on a common CPU type or supported versions of FreeBSD or Solaris<a href="#FOOT129" id="DOCF129" class="footnote"><sup>129</sup></a> you can use `valgrind` (<a href="https://valgrind.org/" class="uref">https://valgrind.org/</a>, pronounced to rhyme with ‘tinned’) to check for possible problems. To run some examples under `valgrind` use something like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
R -d valgrind --vanilla < mypkg-Ex.R
R -d "valgrind --tool=memcheck --leak-check=full" --vanilla < mypkg-Ex.R
```

</div>

where `mypkg-Ex.R` is a set of examples, e.g. the file created in `mypkg.Rcheck` by `R CMD check`. Occasionally this reports memory reads of ‘uninitialised values’ that are the result of compiler optimization, so can be worth checking under an unoptimized compile: for maximal information use a build with debugging symbols. We know there will be some small memory leaks from `readline` and R itself — these are memory areas that are in use right up to the end of the R session. Expect this to run around 20x slower than without `valgrind`, and in some cases much slower than that. Several versions of `valgrind` were not happy with some optimized BLAS libraries that use <span class="abbr acronym">CPU</span>-specific instructions so you may need to build a version of R specifically to use with `valgrind`.

On platforms where `valgrind` and its headers<a href="#FOOT130" id="DOCF130" class="footnote"><sup>130</sup></a> are installed you can build a version of R with extra instrumentation to help `valgrind` detect errors in the use of memory allocated from the R heap. The `configure` option is `--with-valgrind-instrumentation=``level`, where `level` is 0, 1 or 2. Level 0 is the default and does not add anything. Level 1 will detect some uses<a href="#FOOT131" id="DOCF131" class="footnote"><sup>131</sup></a> of uninitialised memory and has little impact on speed (compared to level 0). Level 2 will detect many other memory-use bugs<a href="#FOOT132" id="DOCF132" class="footnote"><sup>132</sup></a> but make R much slower when running under `valgrind`. Using this in conjunction with `gctorture` can be even more effective (and even slower).

An example of `valgrind` output is

<div class="example smallexample">

``` example-preformatted
==12539== Invalid read of size 4
==12539==    at 0x1CDF6CBE: csc_compTr (Mutils.c:273)
==12539==    by 0x1CE07E1E: tsc_transpose (dtCMatrix.c:25)
==12539==    by 0x80A67A7: do_dotcall (dotcode.c:858)
==12539==    by 0x80CACE2: Rf_eval (eval.c:400)
==12539==    by 0x80CB5AF: R_execClosure (eval.c:658)
==12539==    by 0x80CB98E: R_execMethod (eval.c:760)
==12539==    by 0x1B93DEFA: R_standardGeneric (methods_list_dispatch.c:624)
==12539==    by 0x810262E: do_standardGeneric (objects.c:1012)
==12539==    by 0x80CAD23: Rf_eval (eval.c:403)
==12539==    by 0x80CB2F0: Rf_applyClosure (eval.c:573)
==12539==    by 0x80CADCC: Rf_eval (eval.c:414)
==12539==    by 0x80CAA03: Rf_eval (eval.c:362)
==12539==  Address 0x1C0D2EA8 is 280 bytes inside a block of size 1996 alloc'd
==12539==    at 0x1B9008D1: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:149)
==12539==    by 0x80F1B34: GetNewPage (memory.c:610)
==12539==    by 0x80F7515: Rf_allocVector (memory.c:1915)
...
```

</div>

This example is from an instrumented version of R, while tracking down a bug in the <a href="https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=Matrix" class="url"><strong>Matrix</strong></a> package in 2006. The first line indicates that R has tried to read 4 bytes from a memory address that it does not have access to. This is followed by a C stack trace showing where the error occurred. Next is a description of the memory that was accessed. It is inside a block allocated by `malloc`, called from `GetNewPage`, that is, in the internal R heap. Since this memory all belongs to R, `valgrind` would not (and did not) detect the problem in an uninstrumented build of R. In this example the stack trace was enough to isolate and fix the bug, which was in `tsc_transpose`, and in this example running under `gctorture()` did not provide any additional information.

`valgrind` is good at spotting the use of uninitialized values: use option `--track-origins=yes` to show where these originated from. What it cannot detect is the misuse of arrays allocated on the stack: this includes C automatic variables and some<a href="#FOOT133" id="DOCF133" class="footnote"><sup>133</sup></a> Fortran arrays.

It is possible to run all the examples, tests and vignettes covered by `R CMD check` under `valgrind` by using the option `--use-valgrind`. If you do this you will need to select the `valgrind` options some other way, for example by having a `~/.valgrindrc` file containing

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
--leak-check=full
--track-origins=yes
```

</div>

or setting the environment variable `VALGRIND_OPTS`. As from R 4.2.0, `--use-valgrind` also uses `valgrind` when re-building the vignettes.

This section has described the use of `memtest`, the default (and most useful) of `valgrind`’s tools. There are others described in its documentation: `helgrind` can be useful for threaded programs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Using-Address-Sanitizer" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-Undefined-Behaviour-Sanitizer" rel="next">Using the Undefined Behaviour Sanitizer</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-valgrind" rel="prev">Using Valgrind</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Checking-memory-access" rel="up">Checking memory access</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.3.3 Using the Address Sanitizer <a href="#Using-the-Address-Sanitizer" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

`AddressSanitizer` (‘<span class="abbr abbr">ASan</span>’) is a tool with similar aims to the memory checker in `valgrind`. It is available with suitable builds<a href="#FOOT134" id="DOCF134" class="footnote"><sup>134</sup></a> of `gcc` and `clang` on common Linux and macOS platforms. See <a href="https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UsersManual.html#controlling-code-generation" class="uref">https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UsersManual.html#controlling-code-generation</a>, <a href="https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html" class="uref">https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html</a> and <a href="https://github.com/google/sanitizers" class="uref">https://github.com/google/sanitizers</a>.

More thorough checks of C++ code are done if the C++ library has been ‘annotated’: at the time of writing this applied to `std::vector` in `libc++` for use with `clang` and gives rise to ‘`container-overflow`’<a href="#FOOT135" id="DOCF135" class="footnote"><sup>135</sup></a> reports.

It requires code to have been compiled *and linked* with `-fsanitize=address` and compiling with `-fno-omit-frame-pointer` will give more legible reports. It has a runtime penalty of 2–3x, extended compilation times and uses substantially more memory, often 1–2GB, at run time. On 64-bit platforms it reserves (but does not allocate) 16–20TB of virtual memory: restrictive shell settings can cause problems. It can be helpful to increase the stack size, for example to 40MB.

By comparison with `valgrind`, <span class="abbr abbr">ASan</span> can detect misuse of stack and global variables but not the use of uninitialized memory.

Recent versions return symbolic addresses for the location of the error provided `llvm-symbolizer`<a href="#FOOT136" id="DOCF136" class="footnote"><sup>136</sup></a> is on the path: if it is available but not on the path or has been renamed<a href="#FOOT137" id="DOCF137" class="footnote"><sup>137</sup></a>, one can use an environment variable, e.g.

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
ASAN_SYMBOLIZER_PATH=/path/to/llvm-symbolizer
```

</div>

An alternative is to pipe the output through `asan_symbolize.py`<a href="#FOOT138" id="DOCF138" class="footnote"><sup>138</sup></a> and perhaps then (for compiled C++ code) `c++filt`. (On macOS, you may need to run `dsymutil` to get line-number reports.)

The simplest way to make use of this is to build a version of R with something like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
CC="gcc -std=gnu99 -fsanitize=address"
CFLAGS="-fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O2 -Wall -pedantic -mtune=native"
```

</div>

which will ensure that the `libasan` run-time library is compiled into the R executable. However this check can be enabled on a per-package basis by using a `~/.R/Makevars` file like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
CC = gcc -std=gnu99 -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer
CXX = g++ -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer
FC = gfortran -fsanitize=address
```

</div>

(Note that `-fsanitize=address` has to be part of the compiler specification to ensure it is used for linking. These settings will not be honoured by packages which ignore `~/.R/Makevars`.) It will be necessary to build R with

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
MAIN_LDFLAGS = -fsanitize=address
```

</div>

to link the runtime libraries into the R executable if it was not specified as part of ‘`CC`’ when R was built. (For some builds without <span class="abbr abbr">OpenMP</span>, `-pthread` is also required.)

For options available *via* the environment variable `ASAN_OPTIONS` see <a href="https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerFlags" class="uref">https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerFlags</a>. With `gcc` additional control is available *via* the `--param` flag: see its `man` page.

For more detailed information on an error, R can be run under a debugger with a breakpoint set before the address sanitizer report is produced: for `gdb` or `lldb` you could use

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
break __asan_report_error
```

</div>

(See <a href="https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerAndDebugger" class="uref">https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerAndDebugger</a>.)

More recent versions<a href="#FOOT139" id="DOCF139" class="footnote"><sup>139</sup></a> added the flag `-fsanitize-address-use-after-scope`: see <a href="https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerUseAfterScope" class="uref">https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerUseAfterScope</a>.

One of the checks done by <span class="abbr abbr">ASan</span> is that `malloc/free` and in C++ `new/delete` and `new[]/delete[]` are used consistently (rather than say `free` being used to deallocate memory allocated by `new[]`). This matters on some systems but not all: unfortunately on some of those where it does not matter, system libraries<a href="#FOOT140" id="DOCF140" class="footnote"><sup>140</sup></a> are not consistent. The check can be suppressed by including ‘`alloc_dealloc_mismatch=0`’ in `ASAN_OPTIONS`.

<span class="abbr abbr">ASan</span> also checks system calls and sometimes reports can refer to problems in the system software and not the package nor R. A couple of reports have been of ‘heap-use-after-free’ errors in the X11 libraries called from Tcl/Tk.

Apple provide a version of the address sanitizer in recent versions of its C/C++ compiler. This will probably give messages about ‘malloc: nano zone abandoned’ which are innocuous and can be suppressed by setting environment variable `MallocNanoZone` to `0`. It can be helpful to install debug symbols (`INSTALL --dsym` for the package under test and particularly for reverse dependencies.

For more detail on using sanitizers with macOS see <a href="https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/bdr/M1-SAN/README.txt" class="uref">https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/bdr/M1-SAN/README.txt</a>.

- [Using the Leak Sanitizer](#Using-Leak-Sanitizer)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<div id="Using-Leak-Sanitizer" class="subsubsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-Address-Sanitizer" rel="up">Using the Address Sanitizer</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.3.3.1 Using the Leak Sanitizer <a href="#Using-the-Leak-Sanitizer" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

For `x86_64` Linux there is a leak sanitizer, ‘<span class="abbr abbr">LSan</span>’: see <a href="https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerLeakSanitizer" class="uref">https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerLeakSanitizer</a>. This is available on recent versions of `gcc` and `clang`, and where available is compiled in as part of <span class="abbr abbr">ASan</span>.

One way to invoke this from an <span class="abbr abbr">ASan</span>-enabled build is by the environment variable

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
ASAN_OPTIONS='detect_leaks=1'
```

</div>

However, this was made the default as from LLVM `clang` 3.5 and `gcc` 5.1.0.

When <span class="abbr abbr">LSan</span> is enabled, leaks give the process a failure error status (by default `23`). For an R package this means the R process, and as the parser retains some memory to the end of the process, if R itself was built against <span class="abbr abbr">ASan</span> all runs will have a failure error status (which may include running R as part of building R itself).

To disable this, allocation-mismatch checking and some strict C++ checking use

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
setenv ASAN_OPTIONS 'alloc_dealloc_mismatch=0:detect_leaks=0:detect_odr_violation=0'
```

</div>

The leak sanitizer is not part of <span class="abbr abbr">ASan</span> in the Apple `clang` implementation.

<span class="abbr abbr">LSan</span> also has a ‘stand-alone’ mode where it is compiled in using `-fsanitize=leak` and avoids the run-time overhead of <span class="abbr abbr">ASan</span>.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

</div>

<div id="Using-Undefined-Behaviour-Sanitizer" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Other-analyses-with-_0060clang_0027" rel="next">Other analyses with ‘clang’</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-Address-Sanitizer" rel="prev">Using the Address Sanitizer</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Checking-memory-access" rel="up">Checking memory access</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.3.4 Using the Undefined Behaviour Sanitizer <a href="#Using-the-Undefined-Behaviour-Sanitizer" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

‘Undefined behaviour’ is where the language standard does not require particular behaviour from the compiler. Examples include division by zero (where for doubles R requires the <span class="abbr acronym">ISO</span>/<span class="abbr acronym">IEC</span> 60559 behaviour but C/C++ do not), use of zero-length arrays, shifts too far for signed types (e.g. `int x, y; y = x << 31;`), out-of-range coercion, invalid C++ casts and mis-alignment. Not uncommon examples of out-of-range coercion in R packages are attempts to coerce a `NaN` or infinity to type `int` or `NA_INTEGER` to an unsigned type such as `size_t`. Also common is `y[x - 1]` forgetting that `x` might be `NA_INTEGER`.

‘UBSanitizer’ is a tool for C/C++ source code selected by `-fsanitize=undefined` in suitable builds<a href="#FOOT141" id="DOCF141" class="footnote"><sup>141</sup></a> of `clang` and GCC. Its (main) runtime library is linked into each package’s DLL, so it is less often needed to be included in `MAIN_LDFLAGS`. Platforms supported by `clang` are listed at <a href="https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.html#supported-platforms" class="uref">https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.html#supported-platforms</a>: <span class="abbr acronym">CRAN</span> uses it for C/C++ with both GCC and `clang` on ‘`x86_64`’ Linux: the two toolchains often highlight different things with more reports from `clang` than GCC.

This sanitizer may be combined with the Address Sanitizer by `-fsanitize=undefined,address` (where both are supported, and we have seen library conflicts for `clang` 17 and later).

Finer control of what is checked can be achieved by other options.

For `clang` see <a href="https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.html#ubsan-checks" class="uref">https://clang.llvm.org/docs/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.html#ubsan-checks</a>. The current set is (on a single line):

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
-fsanitize=alignment,bool,bounds,builtin,enum,float-cast-overflow,
float-divide-by-zero,function,implicit-unsigned-integer-truncation,
implicit-signed-integer-truncation,implicit-integer-sign-change,
integer-divide-by-zero,nonnull-attribute,null,nullability-arg,
nullability-assign,nullability-return,object-size,
pointer-overflow,return,returns-nonnull-attribute,shift,
signed-integer-overflow,unreachable,unsigned-integer-overflow,
unsigned-shift-base,vla-bound,vptr
```

</div>

(plus the more specific versions `array-bounsds`, `local-bounds`, `shift-base` and `shift-exponent`), or use something like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
-fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize=float-divide-by-zero
```

</div>

where in recent versions `-fno-sanitize=float-divide-by-zero` is the default.

Options `return` and `vptr` apply only to C++: to use `vptr` its run-time library needs to be linked into the main R executable by building the latter with something like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
MAIN_LD="clang++ -fsanitize=undefined"
```

</div>

Option `float-divide-by-zero` is undesirable for use with R which allow such divisions as part of <span class="abbr acronym">IEC</span> 60559 arithmetic, and in versions of `clang` since June 2019 it is no longer part of `-fsanitize=undefined`.

There are also groups of options `implicit-integer-truncation`, `mplicit-integer-arithmetic-value-change`, `implicit-conversion`, `integer` and `nullability`.

For GCC see <a href="https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Instrumentation-Options.html" class="uref">https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Instrumentation-Options.html</a> (or the manual for your version of GCC, installed or *via* <a href="https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/" class="uref">https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/</a>: look for ‘Program Instrumentation Options’) for the options supported by GCC: versions 13.x supported

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
-fsanitize=alignment,bool,bounds,builtin,enum,integer-divide-by-zero,
nonnull-attribute,null,object-size,pointer-overflow,return,
returns-nonnull-attribute,shift,signed-integer-overflow,
unreachable,vla-bound,vptr
```

</div>

plus the more specific versions `shift-base` and `shift-exponent` and non-default options

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
bounds-strict,float-cast-overflow,float-divide-by-zero
```

</div>

where `float-divide-by-zero` is not desirable for R uses and `bounds-strict` is an extension of `bounds`.

Other useful flags include

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
-no-fsanitize-recover
```

</div>

which causes the first report to be fatal (it always is for the `unreachable` and `return` suboptions). For more detailed information on where the runtime error occurs, using

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
setenv UBSAN_OPTIONS 'print_stacktrace=1'
```

</div>

will include a traceback in the report. Beyond that, R can be run under a debugger with a breakpoint set before the sanitizer report is produced: for `gdb` or `lldb` you could use

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
break __ubsan_handle_float_cast_overflow
break __ubsan_handle_float_cast_overflow_abort
```

</div>

or similar (there are handlers for each type of undefined behaviour).

There are also the compiler flags `-fcatch-undefined-behavior` and `-ftrapv`, said to be more reliable in `clang` than `gcc`.

For more details on the topic see <a href="https://blog.regehr.org/archives/213" class="uref">https://blog.regehr.org/archives/213</a> and <a href="https://blog.llvm.org/2011/05/what-every-c-programmer-should-know.html" class="uref">https://blog.llvm.org/2011/05/what-every-c-programmer-should-know.html</a> (which has 3 parts).

It may or may not be possible to build R itself with `-fsanitize=undefined`: problems have in the past been seen with <span class="abbr abbr">OpenMP</span>-using code with `gcc` but there has been success with LLVM `clang` up to version 16.. However, problems have been seen with LLVM `clang` 17 and later, including missing entry points and R builds hanging. What has succeeded is to use <span class="abbr abbr">UBSAN</span> just for the package under test (and not in combination with <span class="abbr abbr">ASAN</span>). To do so, check with an unaltered R, using a custom `Makevars` file something like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
CC = clang -fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize=float-divide-by-zero -fno-omit-frame-pointer
CXX = clang++ -fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize=float-divide-by-zero -fno-omit-frame-pointer -frtti

UBSAN_DIR = /path/to/LLVM18/lib/clang/18/lib/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
SAN_LIBS = $(UBSAN_DIR)/libclang_rt.ubsan_standalone.a $(UBSAN_DIR)/libclang_rt.ubsan_standalone_cxx.a
```

</div>

which links the <span class="abbr abbr">UBSAN</span> libraries statically into the package-under-test’s <span class="abbr abbr">DSO</span>. It is also possible to use the dynamic library *via*

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SAN_LIBS = -L$(UBSAN_DIR) -Wl,-rpath,$(UBSAN_DIR) -lclang_rt.ubsan_standalone
```

</div>

provided `UBSAN_DIR` is added to the runtime library path (as shown or using `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`). **N.B.**: The details, especially the paths used, have changed several times recently.

Apple provides a version of the undefined behaviour sanitizer in recent versions of its C/C++ compiler. For more detail on using sanitizers with macOS see <a href="https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/bdr/M1-SAN/README.txt" class="uref">https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/bdr/M1-SAN/README.txt</a>.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Other-analyses-with-_0060clang_0027" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Other-analyses-with-_0060gcc_0027" rel="next">Other analyses with ‘gcc’</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-Undefined-Behaviour-Sanitizer" rel="prev">Using the Undefined Behaviour Sanitizer</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Checking-memory-access" rel="up">Checking memory access</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.3.5 Other analyses with ‘clang’ <a href="#Other-analyses-with-_0060clang_0027-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

Recent versions of LLVM `clang` on Linux have ‘ThreadSanitizer’ (<a href="https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki#threadsanitizer" class="uref">https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki#threadsanitizer</a>), a ‘data race detector for C/C++ programs’, and ‘MemorySanitizer’ (<a href="https://clang.llvm.org/docs/MemorySanitizer.html" class="uref">https://clang.llvm.org/docs/MemorySanitizer.html</a>, <a href="https://github.com/google/sanitizers" class="uref">https://github.com/google/sanitizers</a>) for the detection of uninitialized memory. Both are based on and provide similar functionality to tools in `valgrind`. The ThreadSanitizer is also available for Apple `clang` on macOS.

`clang` has a ‘Static Analyzer’ which can be run on the source files during compilation: see <a href="https://clang-analyzer.llvm.org/" class="uref">https://clang-analyzer.llvm.org/</a>.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Other-analyses-with-_0060gcc_0027" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-_0060Dr_002e-Memory_0027" rel="next">Using ‘Dr. Memory’</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Other-analyses-with-_0060clang_0027" rel="prev">Other analyses with ‘clang’</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Checking-memory-access" rel="up">Checking memory access</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.3.6 Other analyses with ‘gcc’ <a href="#Other-analyses-with-_0060gcc_0027-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

GCC 10 introduced a new flag `-fanalyzer` which does static analysis during compilation, currently for C code. It is regarded as *experimental* and it may slow down computation considerably when problems are found (and use many GB of resident memory). There is some overlap with problems detected by the Undefined Behaviour sanitizer, but some issues are only reported by this tool and as it is a static analysis, it does not rely on code paths being exercised.

See <a href="https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-10.1.0/gcc/Static-Analyzer-Options.html" class="uref">https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-10.1.0/gcc/Static-Analyzer-Options.html</a> (or the documentation for your version of `gcc` if later) and <a href="https://developers.redhat.com/blog/2020/03/26/static-analysis-in-gcc-10" class="uref">https://developers.redhat.com/blog/2020/03/26/static-analysis-in-gcc-10</a>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Using-_0060Dr_002e-Memory_0027" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Fortran-array-bounds-checking" rel="next">Fortran array bounds checking</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Other-analyses-with-_0060gcc_0027" rel="prev">Other analyses with ‘gcc’</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Checking-memory-access" rel="up">Checking memory access</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.3.7 Using ‘Dr. Memory’ <a href="#Using-_0060Dr_002e-Memory_0027-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

‘Dr. Memory’ from <a href="https://drmemory.org/" class="uref">https://drmemory.org/</a> is a memory checker for (currently) Windows, Linux and macOS with similar aims to `valgrind`. It works with unmodified executables<a href="#FOOT142" id="DOCF142" class="footnote"><sup>142</sup></a> and detects memory access errors, uninitialized reads and memory leaks.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Fortran-array-bounds-checking" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-_0060Dr_002e-Memory_0027" rel="prev">Using ‘Dr. Memory’</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Checking-memory-access" rel="up">Checking memory access</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.3.8 Fortran array bounds checking <a href="#Fortran-array-bounds-checking-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

Most of the Fortran compilers used with R allow code to be compiled with checking of array bounds: for example `gfortran` has option `-fbounds-check`. This will give an error when the upper or lower bound is exceeded, e.g.

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
At line 97 of file .../src/appl/dqrdc2.f
Fortran runtime error: Index '1' of dimension 1 of array 'x' above upper bound of 0
```

</div>

One does need to be aware that lazy programmers often specify Fortran dimensions as `1` rather than `*` or a real bound and these will be reported (as may `*` dimensions)

It is easy to arrange to use this check on just the code in your package: add to `~/.R/Makevars` something like (for `gfortran`)

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
FFLAGS = -g -O2 -mtune=native -fbounds-check
```

</div>

when you run `R CMD check`.

This may report errors with the way that Fortran character variables are passed, particularly when Fortran subroutines are called from C code and character lengths are not passed (see <a href="#Fortran-character-strings" class="pxref">Fortran character strings</a>).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

</div>

<div id="Debugging-compiled-code" class="section-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Using-Link_002dtime-Optimization" rel="next">Using Link-time Optimization</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Checking-memory-access" rel="prev">Checking memory access</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Debugging" rel="up">Debugging</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

### 4.4 Debugging compiled code <a href="#Debugging-compiled-code-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Debugging" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Sooner or later programmers will be faced with the need to debug compiled code loaded into R. This section is geared to platforms using `gdb` with code compiled by `gcc`, but similar things are possible with other debuggers such as `lldb` (<a href="https://lldb.llvm.org/" class="uref">https://lldb.llvm.org/</a>, used on macOS) and Sun’s `dbx`: some debuggers have graphical front-ends available.

Consider first ‘crashes’, that is when R terminated unexpectedly with an illegal memory access (a ‘segfault’ or ‘bus error’), illegal instruction or similar. Unix-alike versions of R use a signal handler which aims to give some basic information. For example

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
 *** caught segfault ***
address 0x20000028, cause 'memory not mapped'

Traceback:
 1: .identC(class1[[1]], class2)
 2: possibleExtends(class(sloti), classi, ClassDef2 = getClassDef(classi,
where = where))
 3: validObject(t(cu))
 4: stopifnot(validObject(cu <- as(tu, "dtCMatrix")), validObject(t(cu)),
validObject(t(tu)))

Possible actions:
1: abort (with core dump)
2: normal R exit
3: exit R without saving workspace
4: exit R saving workspace
Selection: 3
```

</div>

Since the R process may be damaged, the only really safe options are the first or third. (Note that a core dump is only produced where enabled: a common default in a shell is to limit its size to 0, thereby disabling it.)

A fairly common cause of such crashes is a package which uses `.C` or `.Fortran` and writes beyond (at either end) one of the arguments it is passed. There is a good way to detect this: using `options(CBoundsCheck = TRUE)` (which can be selected *via* the environment variable `R_C_BOUNDS_CHECK=yes)` changes the way `.C` and `.Fortran` work to check if the compiled code writes in the 64 bytes at either end of an argument.

Another cause of a ‘crash’ is to overrun the C stack. R tries to track that in its own code, but it may happen in third-party compiled code. For modern POSIX-compliant OSes R can safely catch that and return to the top-level prompt, so one gets something like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
> .C("aaa")
Error: segfault from C stack overflow
>
```

</div>

However, C stack overflows are fatal under Windows and normally defeat attempts at debugging on that platform. Further, the size of the stack is set when R is compiled on Windows, whereas on POSIX OSes it can be set in the shell from which R is launched.

If you have a crash which gives a core dump you can use something like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
gdb /path/to/R/bin/exec/R core.12345
```

</div>

to examine the core dump. If core dumps are disabled or to catch errors that do not generate a dump one can run R directly under a debugger by for example

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
$ R -d gdb --vanilla
...
gdb> run
```

</div>

at which point R will run normally, and hopefully the debugger will catch the error and return to its prompt. This can also be used to catch infinite loops or interrupt very long-running code. For a simple example

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
> for(i in 1:1e7) x <- rnorm(100)
[hit Ctrl-C]
Program received signal SIGINT, Interrupt.
0x00397682 in _int_free () from /lib/tls/libc.so.6
(gdb) where
#0  0x00397682 in _int_free () from /lib/tls/libc.so.6
#1  0x00397eba in free () from /lib/tls/libc.so.6
#2  0xb7cf2551 in R_gc_internal (size_needed=313)
    at /users/ripley/R/svn/R-devel/src/main/memory.c:743
#3  0xb7cf3617 in Rf_allocVector (type=13, length=626)
    at /users/ripley/R/svn/R-devel/src/main/memory.c:1906
#4  0xb7c3f6d3 in PutRNGstate ()
    at /users/ripley/R/svn/R-devel/src/main/RNG.c:351
#5  0xb7d6c0a5 in do_random2 (call=0x94bf7d4, op=0x92580e8, args=0x9698f98,
    rho=0x9698f28) at /users/ripley/R/svn/R-devel/src/main/random.c:183
...
```

</div>

In many cases it is possible to attach a debugger to a running process: this is helpful if an alternative front-end is in use or to investigate a task that seems to be taking far too long. This is done by something like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
gdb -p pid
```

</div>

where `pid` is the id of the R executable or front-end process and can be found from within a running R process by calling `Sys.getpid()` or from a process monitor. This stops the process so its state can be examined: use `continue` to resume execution.

Some “tricks” worth knowing follow:

- [Finding entry points in dynamically loaded code](#Finding-entry-points)
- [Inspecting R objects when debugging](#Inspecting-R-objects)
- [Debugging on macOS](#Debugging-on-macOS)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<div id="Finding-entry-points" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Inspecting-R-objects" rel="next">Inspecting R objects when debugging</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Debugging-compiled-code" rel="up">Debugging compiled code</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.4.1 Finding entry points in dynamically loaded code <a href="#Finding-entry-points-in-dynamically-loaded-code" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

Under most compilation environments, compiled code dynamically loaded into R cannot have breakpoints set within it until it is loaded. To use a symbolic debugger on such dynamically loaded code under Unix-alikes use

- Call the debugger on the R executable, for example by <span class="kbd kbd">R -d gdb</span>.
- Start R.
- At the R prompt, use `dyn.load` or `library` to load your shared object.
- Send an interrupt signal. This will put you back to the debugger prompt.
- Set the breakpoints in your code.
- Continue execution of R by typing <span class="kbd kbd">signal 0</span> and hitting return (<span class="kbd key">RET</span>).

Under Windows signals may not be able to be used, and if so the procedure is more complicated. See the rw-FAQ.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Inspecting-R-objects" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Debugging-on-macOS" rel="next">Debugging on macOS</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Finding-entry-points" rel="prev">Finding entry points in dynamically loaded code</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Debugging-compiled-code" rel="up">Debugging compiled code</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.4.2 Inspecting R objects when debugging <a href="#Inspecting-R-objects-when-debugging" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Inspecting-R-objects-when-debugging" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The key to inspecting R objects from compiled code is the function `Rf_PrintValue(SEXP ``s``)` which uses the normal R printing mechanisms to print the R object pointed to by `s`, or `R_PV(SEXP ``s``)` which will only print ‘objects’. <span id="index-Rf_005fPrintValue" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fPrintValue-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

One way to make use of `Rf_PrintValue` is to insert suitable calls into the code to be debugged.

Another way is to call `R_PV` from the symbolic debugger. For example, from `gdb` we can use

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
(gdb) p R_PV(ab)
```

</div>

using the object `ab` from the convolution example, if we have placed a suitable breakpoint in the convolution C code.

To examine an arbitrary R object we need to work a little harder. For example, let

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
R> DF <- data.frame(a = 1:3, b = 4:6)
```

</div>

By setting a breakpoint at `do_get` and typing <span class="kbd kbd">get("DF")</span> at the R prompt, one can find out the address in memory of `DF`, for example

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
Value returned is $1 = (SEXPREC *) 0x40583e1c
(gdb) p *$1
$2 = {
  sxpinfo = {type = 19, obj = 1, named = 1, gp = 0,
    mark = 0, debug = 0, trace = 0, = 0},
  attrib = 0x40583e80,
  u = {
    vecsxp = {
      length = 2,
      type = {c = 0x40634700 "0>X@D>X@0>X@", i = 0x40634700,
        f = 0x40634700, z = 0x40634700, s = 0x40634700},
      truelength = 1075851272,
    },
    primsxp = {offset = 2},
    symsxp = {pname = 0x2, value = 0x40634700, internal = 0x40203008},
    listsxp = {carval = 0x2, cdrval = 0x40634700, tagval = 0x40203008},
    envsxp = {frame = 0x2, enclos = 0x40634700},
    closxp = {formals = 0x2, body = 0x40634700, env = 0x40203008},
    promsxp = {value = 0x2, expr = 0x40634700, env = 0x40203008}
  }
}
```

</div>

</div>

(Debugger output reformatted for better legibility).

Using `R_PV()` one can “inspect” the values of the various elements of the `SEXP`, for example,

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
(gdb) p R_PV($1->attrib)
$names
[1] "a" "b"

$row.names
[1] "1" "2" "3"

$class
[1] "data.frame"

$3 = void
```

</div>

</div>

To find out where exactly the corresponding information is stored, one needs to go “deeper”:

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
(gdb) set $a = $1->attrib
(gdb) p $a->u.listsxp.tagval->u.symsxp.pname->u.vecsxp.type.c
$4 = 0x405d40e8 "names"
(gdb) p $a->u.listsxp.carval->u.vecsxp.type.s[1]->u.vecsxp.type.c
$5 = 0x40634378 "b"
(gdb) p $1->u.vecsxp.type.s[0]->u.vecsxp.type.i[0]
$6 = 1
(gdb) p $1->u.vecsxp.type.s[1]->u.vecsxp.type.i[1]
$7 = 5
```

</div>

</div>

Another alternative is the `R_inspect` function which shows the low-level structure of the objects recursively (addresses differ from the above as this example is created on another machine):

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
(gdb) p R_inspect($1)
@100954d18 19 VECSXP g0c2 [OBJ,NAM(2),ATT] (len=2, tl=0)
  @100954d50 13 INTSXP g0c2 [NAM(2)] (len=3, tl=0) 1,2,3
  @100954d88 13 INTSXP g0c2 [NAM(2)] (len=3, tl=0) 4,5,6
ATTRIB:
  @102a70140 02 LISTSXP g0c0 []
    TAG: @10083c478 01 SYMSXP g0c0 [MARK,NAM(2),gp=0x4000] "names"
    @100954dc0 16 STRSXP g0c2 [NAM(2)] (len=2, tl=0)
      @10099df28 09 CHARSXP g0c1 [MARK,gp=0x21] "a"
      @10095e518 09 CHARSXP g0c1 [MARK,gp=0x21] "b"
    TAG: @100859e60 01 SYMSXP g0c0 [MARK,NAM(2),gp=0x4000] "row.names"
    @102a6f868 13 INTSXP g0c1 [NAM(2)] (len=2, tl=1) -2147483648,-3
    TAG: @10083c948 01 SYMSXP g0c0 [MARK,gp=0x4000] "class"
    @102a6f838 16 STRSXP g0c1 [NAM(2)] (len=1, tl=1)
      @1008c6d48 09 CHARSXP g0c2 [MARK,gp=0x21,ATT] "data.frame"
```

</div>

</div>

In general the representation of each object follows the format:

<div class="example smallexample">

``` example-preformatted
@<address> <type-nr> <type-name> <gc-info> [<flags>] ...
```

</div>

For a more fine-grained control over the depth of the recursion and the output of vectors `R_inspect3` takes additional two character() parameters: maximum depth and the maximal number of elements that will be printed for scalar vectors. The defaults in `R_inspect` are currently -1 (no limit) and 5 respectively.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Debugging-on-macOS" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Inspecting-R-objects" rel="prev">Inspecting R objects when debugging</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Debugging-compiled-code" rel="up">Debugging compiled code</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 4.4.3 Debugging on macOS <a href="#Debugging-on-macOS-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

To debug code in a package it is easiest to unpack it in a directory and install it with

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
R CMD INSTALL --dsym pkgname
```

</div>

as macOS does not store debugging symbols in the `.so` file. (It is not necessary to have R built with debugging symbols, although compiling the package should be done including `-g` in `CFLAGS` / `CXXFLAGS` / `FFLAGS` / `FCFLAGS` as appropriate.)

Security measures may prevent running a <span class="abbr acronym">CRAN</span> binary distribution of R under `lldb` or attaching this as a debugger (<a href="https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/RMacOSX-FAQ.html#I-cannot-attach-debugger-to-R" class="uref">https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/RMacOSX-FAQ.html#I-cannot-attach-debugger-to-R</a>), although both were possible on High Sierra and are again from R 4.2.0. This can also affect locally compiled builds, where attaching to an interactive R session under Big Sur or Monterey worked in 2022 after giving administrator permission *via* a popup-up. (To debug in what Apple deems a non-interactive session, e.g. logged in remotely, see `man DevToolsSecurity`.)

Debugging a local build of R on macOS can raise additional hurdles as environment variables such as `DYLD_FALLBACK_LIBRARY_PATH` are not usually passed through<a href="#FOOT143" id="DOCF143" class="footnote"><sup>143</sup></a> the `lldb` process, resulting in messages like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
R -d lldb
...
(lldb) run
Process 16828 launched: '/path/to/bin/exec/R' (x86_64)
dyld: Library not loaded: libR.dylib
  Referenced from: /path/to/bin/exec/R
```

</div>

A quick workaround is to symlink the dylibs under `R_HOME/lib` to somewhere where they will be found such as the current working directory. It would be possible to do as the distribution does<a href="#FOOT144" id="DOCF144" class="footnote"><sup>144</sup></a> and use `install_name_tool`, but that would have to be done for all the dylibs including those in packages.

It may be simplest to attach the debugger to a running process (see above). Specifically, run R and when it is at the prompt just before a command that is to be debugged, at a terminal

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
ps -ef | grep exec/R
# identify the PID pid for the next command: it is the second item
lldb -p pid
(lldb) continue
```

</div>

and then return to the R console.

For non-interactive use, one may need `lldb --batch`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

</div>

<div id="Using-Link_002dtime-Optimization" class="section-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Debugging-compiled-code" rel="prev">Debugging compiled code</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Debugging" rel="up">Debugging</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

### 4.5 Using Link-time Optimization <a href="#Using-Link_002dtime-Optimization-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

Where supported, *link time optimization* provides a comprehensive way to check the consistency of calls between Fortran files or between C and Fortran. Use this *via* `R CMD INSTALL --use-LTO` (but that does not apply if there is a `src/Makefile` file or a Windows analogue).

To set up support on a Unix-alike, see <a href="R-admin.html#Link_002dTime-Optimization" data-manual="R-admin">Link-Time Optimization</a> in R Installation and Administration. On Linux using GCC without building R with <span class="abbr abbr">LTO</span> support, it should suffice to set

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
LTO_OPT = -flto
LTO_FC_OPT = -flto
AR = gcc-ar
NM = gcc-nm
```

</div>

in a personal (or site) `Makevars` file: See <a href="R-admin.html#Customizing-package-compilation" data-manual="R-admin">Customizing package compilation</a> in R Installation and Administration for more information.

For Windows, first edit file `etc/${R_ARCH}/Makeconf` to give `LTO_OPT` the value `-flto` or do so in a personal/site `Makevars` file; see also file `src/gnuwin32/README.compilation` in the sources.

For example:

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
boot.f:61: warning: type of 'ddot' does not match original declaration [-Wlto-type-mismatch]
        y(j,i)=ddot(p,x(j,1),n,b(1,j,i),1)
crq.f:1023: note: return value type mismatch
```

</div>

where the package author forgot to declare

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
      double precision ddot
      external ddot
```

</div>

in `boot.f`. That package had its own copy of `ddot`: to detect misuse of the one in R’s BLAS library would have needed R configured with `--enable-lto=check`.

Further examples:

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
rkpk2.f:77:5: warning: type of 'dstup' does not match original declaration [-Wlto-type-mismatch]
      *info, wk)
rkpk1.f:2565:5: note: type mismatch in parameter 14
       subroutine dstup (s, lds, nobs, nnull, qraux, jpvt, y, q, ldqr,
rkpk1.f:2565:5: note: 'dstup' was previously declared here
```

</div>

where the fourteenth argument `dum` was missing in the call.

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
reg.f:78:33: warning: type of 'dqrdc' does not match original declaration [-Wlto-type-mismatch]
       call dqrdc (sr, nobs, nobs, nnull, wk, dum, dum, 0)
dstup.f:20: note: 'dqrdc' was previously declared here
       call dqrdc (s, lds, nobs, nnull, qraux, jpvt, work, 1)
```

</div>

`dqrdc` is a LINPACK routine from R, `jpvt` is an integer array and `work` is a double precision one so `dum` cannot match both. (If `--enable-lto=check` had been used the comparison would have been with the definition in R.)

For Fortran files all in the package, most inconsistencies can be detected by concatenating the Fortran files and compiling the result, sometimes with clearer diagnostics than provided by <span class="abbr abbr">LTO</span>. For our last two examples this gives

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
all.f:2966:72:

      *info, work1)
                                                                        1
Warning: Missing actual argument for argument 'dum' at (1)
```

</div>

and

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
all.f:1663:72:

      *ipvtwk), wk(ikwk), wk(iwork1), wk(iwork2), info)
                                                                        1
Warning: Type mismatch in argument 'jpvt' at (1); passed REAL(8) to INTEGER(4)
```

</div>

On a Unix-alike for a package with a `src/Makefile` file, <span class="abbr abbr">LTO</span> can be enabled by including suitable flags in that file, for example

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
LTO = $(LTO_OPT)
LTO_FC = $(LTO_FC_OPT)
```

</div>

and ensuring these are used for compilation, for example as part of `CFLAGS`, `CXXFLAGS` or `FCFLAGS`. If `R CMD SHLIB` is used for compilation, add `--use-LTO` to its call.

On Windows for a package with a `src/Makefile.ucrt` or `src/Makefile.win` file which includes ‘`"${R_HOME}/etc${R_ARCH}/Makeconf"`’, include

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
LTO = $(LTO_OPT)
```

</div>

or to always use <span class="abbr abbr">LTO</span> however R was built,

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
LTO = -flto
```

</div>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

</div>
