<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Allocating-storage" rel="next">Allocating storage</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.1 Handling the effects of garbage collection <a href="#Handling-the-effects-of-garbage-collection" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Garbage-collection" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-PROTECT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-PROTECT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-UNPROTECT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-UNPROTECT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fprotect" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fprotect-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005funprotect" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005funprotect-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

We need to know a little about the way R handles memory allocation. The memory allocated for R objects is not freed by the user; instead, the memory is from time to time *garbage collected*. That is, some or all of the allocated memory not being used is freed or marked as re-usable.

The R object types are represented by a C structure defined by a typedef `SEXPREC` in `Rinternals.h`. It contains several things among which are pointers to data blocks and to other `SEXPREC`s. A `SEXP` is simply a pointer to a `SEXPREC`.

If you create an R object in your C code, you must tell R that you are using the object by using the `PROTECT` macro on a pointer to the object. This tells R that the object is in use so it is not destroyed during garbage collection. Notice that it is the object which is protected, not the pointer variable. It is a common mistake to believe that if you invoked `PROTECT(``p``)` at some point then `p` is protected from then on, but that is not true once a new object is assigned to `p`.

Protecting an R object automatically protects all the R objects pointed to in the corresponding `SEXPREC`, for example all elements of a protected list are automatically protected.

The programmer is solely responsible for housekeeping the calls to `PROTECT`. There is a corresponding macro `UNPROTECT` that takes as argument an `int` giving the number of objects to unprotect when they are no longer needed. The protection mechanism is stack-based, so `UNPROTECT(``n``)` unprotects the last `n` objects which were protected. The calls to `PROTECT` and `UNPROTECT` must balance when the user’s code returns and should balance in all functions. R will warn about `"stack imbalance in .Call"` (or `.External`) if the housekeeping is wrong.

Here is a small example of creating an R numeric vector in C code:

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

    SEXP ab;
      ....
    ab = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, 2));
    REAL(ab)[0] = 123.45;
    REAL(ab)[1] = 67.89;
    UNPROTECT(1);
```

</div>

</div>

Now, the reader may ask how the R object could possibly get removed during those manipulations, as it is just our C code that is running. As it happens, we can do without the protection in this example, but in general we do not know (nor want to know) what is hiding behind the R macros and functions we use, and any of them might cause memory to be allocated, hence garbage collection and hence our object `ab` to be removed. It is usually wise to err on the side of caution and assume that any of the R macros and functions might remove the object.

In some cases it is necessary to keep better track of whether protection is really needed. Be particularly aware of situations where a large number of objects are generated. The pointer protection stack has a fixed size (default 10,000) and can become full. It is not a good idea then to just `PROTECT` everything in sight and `UNPROTECT` several thousand objects at the end. It will almost invariably be possible to either assign the objects as part of another object (which automatically protects them) or unprotect them immediately after use.

There is a less-used macro `UNPROTECT_PTR(``s``)` that unprotects the object pointed to by the `SEXP` `s`, even if it is not the top item on the pointer protection stack. This macro was introduced for use in the parser, where the code interfacing with the R heap is generated and the generator cannot be configured to insert proper calls to `PROTECT` and `UNPROTECT`. However, `UNPROTECT_PTR` is dangerous to use in combination with `UNPROTECT` when the same object has been protected multiple times. It has been superseded by multi-set based functions `R_PreserveInMSet` and `R_ReleaseFromMSet`, which protect objects in a multi-set created by `R_NewPreciousMSet` and typically itself protected using `PROTECT`. These functions should not be needed outside parsers. <span id="index-UNPROTECT_005fPTR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-UNPROTECT_005fPTR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005funprotect_005fptr" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005funprotect_005fptr-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fPreserveInMSet" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fPreserveInMSet-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fReleaseFromMSet" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fReleaseFromMSet-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fNewPreciousMSet" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fNewPreciousMSet-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Sometimes an object is changed (for example duplicated, coerced or grown) yet the current value needs to be protected. For these cases `PROTECT_WITH_INDEX` saves an index of the protection location that can be used to replace the protected value using `REPROTECT`. <span id="index-PROTECT_005fWITH_005fINDEX" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-PROTECT_005fWITH_005fINDEX-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REPROTECT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REPROTECT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fProtectWithIndex" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fProtectWithIndex-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fReprotect" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fReprotect-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> For example (from the internal code for `optim`)

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
    PROTECT_INDEX ipx;

    ....
    PROTECT_WITH_INDEX(s = Rf_eval(OS->R_fcall, OS->R_env), &ipx);
    REPROTECT(s = Rf_coerceVector(s, REALSXP), ipx);
```

</div>

Note that it is dangerous to mix `UNPROTECT_PTR` also with `PROTECT_WITH_INDEX`, as the former changes the protection locations of objects that were protected after the one being unprotected.

<span id="index-R_005fPreserveObject" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fPreserveObject-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fReleaseObject" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fReleaseObject-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

There is another way to avoid the effects of garbage collection: a call to `R_PreserveObject` adds an object to an internal list of objects not to be collected, and a subsequent call to `R_ReleaseObject` removes it from that list. This provides a way for objects which are not returned as part of R objects to be protected across calls to compiled code: on the other hand it becomes the user’s responsibility to release them when they are no longer needed (and this often requires the use of a finalizer). It is less efficient than the normal protection mechanism, and should be used sparingly.

For functions from packages as well as R to safely co-operate in protecting objects, certain rules have to be followed:

- Pointer-protection balance. Calls to `PROTECT` and `UNPROTECT` should balance in each function. A function may only call `UNPROTECT` or `REPROTECT` on objects it has itself protected. Note that the pointer protection stack balance is restored automatically on non-local transfer of control (See <a href="#Condition-handling-and-cleanup-code" class="ref">Condition handling and cleanup code</a>.), as if a call to `UNPROTECT` was invoked with the right argument.
- Caller protection. It is the responsibility of the caller that all arguments passed to a function are protected and will stay protected for the whole execution of the callee. Typically this is achieved by `PROTECT` and `UNPROTECT` calls.
- Protecting return values. Any R objects returned from a function are unprotected (the callee must maintain pointer-protection balance), and hence should be protected immediately by the caller. To be safe against future code changes, assume that any R object returned from any function may need protection. Note that even when conceptually returning an existing protected object, that object may be duplicated.
- All functions/macros allocate. To be safe against future code changes, assume that any function or macro may allocate and hence garbage collector may run and destroy unprotected objects.

It is always safe and recommended to follow those rules. In fact, several R functions and macros protect their own arguments and some functions do not allocate or do not allocate when used in a certain way, but that is subject to change, so relying on that may be fragile. `PROTECT` and `PROTECT_WITH_INDEX` can be safely called with unprotected arguments and `UNPROTECT` does not allocate.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Allocating-storage" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Details-of-R-types" rel="next">Details of R types</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Garbage-Collection" rel="prev">Handling the effects of garbage collection</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.2 Allocating storage <a href="#Allocating-storage-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Allocating-storage" class="index-entry-id"></span>

For many purposes it is sufficient to allocate R objects and manipulate those. There are quite a few `Rf_alloc``Xxx` functions defined in `Rinternals.h`—you may want to explore them.

<span id="index-Rf_005fallocVector" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocVector-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

One that is commonly used is `Rf_allocVector`, the C-level equivalent of R-level `vector()` and its wrappers such as `integer()` and `character()`. One distinction is that whereas the R functions always initialize the elements of the vector, `Rf_allocVector` only does so for lists, expressions and character vectors (the cases where the elements are themselves R objects). Other useful allocation functions are `Rf_alloc3DArray`, `Rf_allocArray`, and `Rf_allocMatrix`. <span id="index-Rf_005falloc3DArray" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005falloc3DArray-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocArray" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocArray-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocMatrix" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocMatrix-2" class="index-entry-id"></span>

When creating new result objects it can be useful to fill them in with values from an existing object. The functions `Rf_copyVector` and `Rf_copyMatrix` can be used for this. `Rf_copyMostAttributes` can also simplify setting up a result object; it is used internally for results of arithmetic operations. <span id="index-Rf_005fcopyVector" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcopyVector-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcopyMatrix" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcopyMatrix-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcopyMostAttrib" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcopyMostAttrib-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

If storage is required for C objects during the calculations this is best allocated by calling `R_alloc`; see <a href="#Memory-allocation" class="pxref">Memory allocation</a>. All of these memory allocation routines do their own error-checking, so the programmer may assume that they will raise an error and not return if the memory cannot be allocated. <span id="index-R_005falloc" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005falloc-2" class="index-entry-id"></span>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Details-of-R-types" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Attributes" rel="next">Attributes</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Allocating-storage" rel="prev">Allocating storage</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.3 Details of R types <a href="#Details-of-R-types-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Details-of-R-types" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Users of the `Rinternals.h` macros will need to know how the R types are known internally. The different R data types are represented in C by *SEXPTYPE*. Some of these are familiar from R and some are internal data types. The usual R object modes are given in the table.

> | SEXPTYPE  | R equivalent                       |
> |-----------|------------------------------------|
> | `REALSXP` | numeric with storage mode `double` |
> | `INTSXP`  | integer                            |
> | `CPLXSXP` | complex                            |
> | `LGLSXP`  | logical                            |
> | `STRSXP`  | character                          |
> | `VECSXP`  | list (generic vector)              |
> | `LISTSXP` | pairlist                           |
> | `DOTSXP`  | a ‘`…`’ object                     |
> | `NILSXP`  | NULL                               |
> | `SYMSXP`  | name/symbol                        |
> | `CLOSXP`  | function or function closure       |
> | `ENVSXP`  | environment                        |

Among the important internal `SEXPTYPE`s are `LANGSXP`, `CHARSXP`, `PROMSXP`, etc. (**N.B.**: although it is possible to return objects of internal types, it is unsafe to do so as assumptions are made about how they are handled which may be violated at user-level evaluation.) More details are given in <a href="R-ints.html#R-Internal-Structures" data-manual="R-ints">R Internal Structures</a> in R Internals.

Unless you are very sure about the type of the arguments, the code should check the data types. Sometimes it may also be necessary to check data types of objects created by evaluating an R expression in the C code. You can use functions like `Rf_isReal`, `Rf_isInteger` and `Rf_isString` to do type checking. <span id="index-Rf_005fisReal" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisReal-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisInteger" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisInteger-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisString-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> Other such functions declared in the header file `Rinternals.h` include `Rf_isNull`, `Rf_isSymbol`, `Rf_isLogical`, `Rf_isComplex`, `Rf_isExpression`, and `Rf_isEnvironment`. <span id="index-Rf_005fisNull" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisNull-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisSymbol" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisSymbol-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisLogical" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisLogical-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisComplex" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisComplex-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisExpression" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisExpression-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisEnvironment" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisEnvironment-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> All of these take a `SEXP` as argument and return 1 or 0 to indicate `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

What happens if the `SEXP` is not of the correct type? Sometimes you have no other option except to generate an error. You can use the function `Rf_error` for this. It is usually better to coerce the object to the correct type. For example, if you find that an `SEXP` is of the type `INTEGER`, but you need a `REAL` object, you can change the type by using

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
newSexp = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(oldSexp, REALSXP));
```

</div>

<span id="index-Rf_005fcoerceVector" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcoerceVector-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Protection is needed as a new *object* is created; the object formerly pointed to by the `SEXP` is still protected but now unused.<a href="#FOOT162" id="DOCF162" class="footnote"><sup>162</sup></a>

All the coercion functions do their own error-checking, and generate `NA`s with a warning or stop with an error as appropriate.

Note that these coercion functions are *not* the same as calling `as.numeric` (and so on) in R code, as they do not dispatch on the class of the object. Thus it is normally preferable to do the coercion in the calling R code.

So far we have only seen how to create and coerce R objects from C code, and how to extract the numeric data from numeric R vectors. These can suffice to take us a long way in interfacing R objects to numerical algorithms, but we may need to know a little more to create useful return objects.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Attributes" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Classes" rel="next">Classes</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Details-of-R-types" rel="prev">Details of R types</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.4 Attributes <a href="#Attributes-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Attributes" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Many R objects have attributes: some of the most useful are classes and the `dim` and `dimnames` that mark objects as matrices or arrays. It can also be helpful to work with the `names` attribute of vectors.

To illustrate this, let us write code to take the outer product of two vectors (which `outer` and `%o%` already do). As usual the R code is simple

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
out <- function(x, y)
{
    storage.mode(x) <- storage.mode(y) <- "double"
    .Call("out", x, y)
}
```

</div>

where we expect `x` and `y` to be numeric vectors (possibly integer), possibly with names. This time we do the coercion in the calling R code.

C code to do the computations is

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

SEXP out(SEXP x, SEXP y)
{
    int nx = Rf_length(x), ny = Rf_length(y);
    SEXP ans = PROTECT(Rf_allocMatrix(REALSXP, nx, ny));
    double *rx = REAL(x), *ry = REAL(y), *rans = REAL(ans);
    for(int i = 0; i < nx; i++) {
        double tmp = rx[i];
        for(int j = 0; j < ny; j++)
            rans[i + nx*j] = tmp * ry[j];
    }
    UNPROTECT(1);
    return ans;
}
```

</div>

</div>

Note the way `REAL` is used: as it is a function call it can be considerably faster to store the result and index that.

However, we would like to set the `dimnames` of the result. We can use

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP out(SEXP x, SEXP y)
{
    int nx = Rf_length(x), ny = Rf_length(y);
    SEXP ans = PROTECT(Rf_allocMatrix(REALSXP, nx, ny));
    double *rx = REAL(x), *ry = REAL(y), *rans = REAL(ans);

    for(int i = 0; i < nx; i++) {
      double tmp = rx[i];
      for(int j = 0; j < ny; j++)
        rans[i + nx*j] = tmp * ry[j];
    }

    SEXP dimnames = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(VECSXP, 2));
    SET_VECTOR_ELT(dimnames, 0, Rf_getAttrib(x, R_NamesSymbol));
    SET_VECTOR_ELT(dimnames, 1, Rf_getAttrib(y, R_NamesSymbol));
    Rf_setAttrib(ans, R_DimNamesSymbol, dimnames);
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted

```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    UNPROTECT(2);
    return ans;
}
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fNamesSymbol" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fNamesSymbol-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fDimNamesSymbol" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fDimNamesSymbol-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

This example introduces several new features. There are shortcuts here too: the functions `Rf_namesgets`, `Rf_dimgets` and `Rf_dimnamesgets` are the internal versions of the default methods of `names<-`, `dim<-` and `dimnames<-` (for vectors and arrays), and there are functions such as `Rf_GetColNames`, `Rf_GetRowNames`, `Rf_GetMatrixDimnames` and `Rf_GetArrayDimnames`. <span id="index-Rf_005fGetArrayDimnames" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetArrayDimnames-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetMatrixDimnames" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetMatrixDimnames-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetColNames" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetColNames-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetRowNames" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetRowNames-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fnamesgets" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fnamesgets-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fdimnamesgets" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fdimnamesgets-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fdimgets" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fdimgets-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

What happens if we want to add an attribute that is not pre-defined? We need to add a symbol for it *via* a call to <span id="index-Rf_005finstall" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005finstall-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> `Rf_install`. Suppose for illustration we wanted to add an attribute `"version"` with value `3.0`. We could use

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP version;
version = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, 1));
REAL(version)[0] = 3.0;
Rf_setAttrib(ans, Rf_install("version"), version);
UNPROTECT(1);
```

</div>

</div>

Using `Rf_install` when it is not needed is harmless and provides a simple way to retrieve the symbol from the symbol table if it is already installed. However, the lookup takes a non-trivial amount of time, so consider code such as

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
static SEXP VerSymbol = NULL;
...
if (VerSymbol == NULL) VerSymbol = Rf_install("version");
```

</div>

if it is to be done frequently.

This example can be simplified by another convenience function:

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP version = PROTECT(Rf_ScalarReal(3.0));
Rf_setAttrib(ans, Rf_install("version"), version);
UNPROTECT(1);
```

</div>

</div>

If a result is to be a vector with all elements named, then `Rf_mkNamed` can be used to allocate a vector of a specified type. Names are provided as a C vector of strings terminated by an empty string:

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
const char *nms[] = {"xi", "yi", "zi", ""};
Rf_mkNamed(VECSXP, nms);
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-Rf_005fmkNamed" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fmkNamed-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Symbols can also be installed or retrieved based on a name in a `CHARSXP` object using either `Rf_installChar` or `Rf_installTrChar`. These used to differ in handling character encoding but have been identical since R 4.0.0. <span id="index-Rf_005finstallChar" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005finstallChar-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005finstallTrChar" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005finstallTrChar-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

#### 5.9.5 Classes <a href="#Classes-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Classes" class="index-entry-id"></span>

In R the class is just the attribute named `"class"` so it can be handled as such, but there is a shortcut `Rf_classgets`. Suppose we want to give the return value in our example the class `"mat"`. We can use

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
      ....
    SEXP ans, dim, dimnames, class;
      ....
    class = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(STRSXP, 1));
    SET_STRING_ELT(class, 0, Rf_mkChar("mat"));
    Rf_classgets(ans, class);
    UNPROTECT(4);
    return ans;
}
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-Rf_005fclassgets" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fclassgets-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

As the value is a character vector, we have to know how to create that from a C character array, which we do using the function `Rf_mkChar`.

Objects without an explicit class can have an implicit class. In R the function `class` returns the explicit or implicit class. The function `R_class` is the `C` equivalent. <span id="index-R_005fclass" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fclass-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

#### 5.9.6 S4 objects <a href="#S4-objects-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-S4-objects" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Several functions are available for working with S4 objects and classes in C, including:

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP Rf_allocS4Object(void);
SEXP Rf_asS4(SEXP, Rboolean, int);
int R_check_class_etc(SEXP x, const char **valid);
SEXP R_do_MAKE_CLASS(const char *what);
SEXP R_do_new_object(SEXP class_def);
SEXP R_do_slot(SEXP obj, SEXP name);
SEXP R_do_slot_assign(SEXP obj, SEXP name, SEXP value);
SEXP R_getClassDef  (const char *what);
int R_has_slot(SEXP obj, SEXP name);
```

</div>

<span id="index-Rf_005fallocS4Object" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocS4Object-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasS4" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasS4-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fcheck_005fclass_005fetc" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fcheck_005fclass_005fetc-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fdo_005fMAKE_005fCLASS" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fdo_005fMAKE_005fCLASS-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fdo_005fnew_005fobject" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fdo_005fnew_005fobject-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fdo_005fslot" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fdo_005fslot-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fdo_005fslot_005fassign" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fdo_005fslot_005fassign-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fgetClassDef" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fgetClassDef-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fhas_005fslot" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fhas_005fslot-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Handling-lists" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-character-data" rel="next">Handling character data</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#S4-objects" rel="prev">S4 objects</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.7 Handling lists <a href="#Handling-lists-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Handling-lists" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Some care is needed with lists, as R moved early on from using LISP-like lists (now called “pairlists”) to S-like generic vectors. As a result, the appropriate test for an object of mode `list` is `Rf_isNewList`, and we need `Rf_allocVector(VECSXP, ``n`) and *not* `Rf_allocList(``n``)`. <span id="index-Rf_005fallocList" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocList-2" class="index-entry-id"></span>

List elements can be retrieved or set by direct access to the elements of the generic vector. Suppose we have a list object

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
a <- list(f = 1, g = 2, h = 3)
```

</div>

Then we can access `a$g` as `a[[2]]` by

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    double g;
      ....
    g = REAL(VECTOR_ELT(a, 1))[0];
```

</div>

</div>

This can rapidly become tedious, and the following function (based on one in package **stats**) is very useful:

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
/* get the list element named str (ASCII), or return NULL */

SEXP getListElement(SEXP list, const char *str)
{
    SEXP elmt = R_NilValue, names = Rf_getAttrib(list, R_NamesSymbol);
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted

```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    for (int i = 0; i < Rf_length(list); i++)
        if(strcmp(CHAR(STRING_ELT(names, i)), str) == 0) {
           /* ASCII only */
           elmt = VECTOR_ELT(list, i);
           break;
        }
    return elmt;
}
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fNilValue" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fNilValue-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

and enables us to say

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
  double g;
  g = REAL(getListElement(a, "g"))[0];
```

</div>

</div>

This code only works for names that are ASCII (see <a href="#Character-encoding-issues" class="pxref">Character encoding issues</a>).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Handling-character-data" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Working-with-closures" rel="next">Working with closures</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-lists" rel="prev">Handling lists</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.8 Handling character data <a href="#Handling-character-data-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-handling-character-data" class="index-entry-id"></span>

R character vectors are stored as `STRSXP`s, a vector type like `VECSXP` where every element is of type `CHARSXP`. The `CHARSXP` elements of `STRSXP`s are accessed using `STRING_ELT` and `SET_STRING_ELT`. <span id="index-STRING_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-STRING_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fSTRING_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fSTRING_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

`CHARSXP`s are read-only objects and must never be modified. In particular, the C-style string contained in a `CHARSXP` should be treated as read-only and for this reason the `CHAR` function used to access the character data of a `CHARSXP` returns `(const char *)` (this also allows compilers to issue warnings about improper use). Since `CHARSXP`s are immutable, the same `CHARSXP` can be shared by any `STRSXP` needing an element representing the same string. R maintains a global cache of `CHARSXP`s so that there is only ever one `CHARSXP` representing a given string in memory. It most cases it is easier to use `Rf_translateChar` or `Rf_translateCharUTF8` to obtain the C string and it is safer against potential future changes in R (see <a href="#Character-encoding-issues" class="pxref">Character encoding issues</a>).

<span id="index-Rf_005fmkChar" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fmkChar-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fmkCharLen" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fmkCharLen-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

You can obtain a `CHARSXP` by calling `Rf_mkChar` and providing a <span class="abbr abbr">NUL</span>-terminated C-style string. This function will return a pre-existing `CHARSXP` if one with a matching string already exists, otherwise it will create a new one and add it to the cache before returning it to you. The variant `Rf_mkCharLen` can be used to create a `CHARSXP` from part of a buffer and will ensure null-termination.

Note that R character strings are restricted to `2^31 - 1` bytes, and hence so should the input to `Rf_mkChar` be (C allows longer strings on 64-bit platforms).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Working-with-closures" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Finding-and-setting-variables" rel="next">Finding and setting variables</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-character-data" rel="prev">Handling character data</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.9 Working with closures <a href="#Working-with-closures-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Working-with-closures" class="index-entry-id"></span>

New function closure objects can be created with `R_mkClosure`:

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP R_mkClosure(SEXP formals, SEXP body, SEXP rho);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fmkClosure" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fmkClosure-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

For creating the formals you can need to use `R_MissingArg` for arguments with no default. <span id="index-R_005fMissingArg" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fMissingArg-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> The components of a closure can be extracted with `R_ClosureFormals`, `R_ClosureBody`, and `R_ClosureEnv`. For a byte compiled closure `R_ClosureBody` returns the compiled body. `R_ClosureExpr` returns the body expression for both compiled and uncompiled closures. The expression for a compiled object can be obtained with `R_BytecodeExpr`. <span id="index-R_005fClosureFormals" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fClosureFormals-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fClosureBody" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fClosureBody-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fClosureEnv" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fClosureEnv-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fClosureExpr" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fClosureExpr-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBytecodeExpr" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBytecodeExpr-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Finding-and-setting-variables" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Some-convenience-functions" rel="next">Some convenience functions</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Working-with-closures" rel="prev">Working with closures</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.10 Finding and setting variables <a href="#Finding-and-setting-variables-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Finding-variables" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Setting-variables" class="index-entry-id"></span>

It will be usual that all the R objects needed in our C computations are passed as arguments to `.Call` or `.External`, but it is possible to find the values of R objects from within the C given their names. The following code is the equivalent of `get(name, envir = rho)`.

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP getvar(SEXP name, SEXP rho)
{
    SEXP ans;

    if (!Rf_isString(name) || Rf_length(name) != 1)
        Rf_error("name is not a single string");
    if (!Rf_isEnvironment(rho))
        Rf_error("rho should be an environment");
    ans = R_getVar(Rf_installChar(STRING_ELT(name, 0)), rho, TRUE);
    if (TYPEOF(ans) != REALSXP || Rf_length(ans) == 0)
        Rf_error("value is not a numeric vector with at least one element");
    Rprintf("first value is %f\n", REAL(ans)[0]);
    return R_NilValue;
}
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-Rf_005finstallChar-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005finstallChar-3" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The main work is done by <span id="index-R_005fgetVar" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fgetVar-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> `R_getVar`, but to use it we need to install `name` as a name in the symbol table. As we wanted the value for internal use, we return `NULL`.

`R_getVar` is similar to the R function `get`. It signals an error if there is no binding for the variable in the environment. `R_getVarEx` can be used to return a default value if no binding is found; this corresponds to the R function `get0`. <span id="index-R_005fgetVarEx" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fgetVarEx-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> The third argument to `R_getVar` and `R_getVarEx` corresponds to the `inherits` argument to the R function `get`:

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP R_getVar(SEXP sym, SEXP rho, Rboolean inherits);
SEXP R_getVarEx(SEXP sym, SEXP rho, Rboolean inherits, SEXP ifnotfound);
```

</div>

</div>

Functions with syntax

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
void Rf_defineVar(SEXP symbol, SEXP value, SEXP rho);
void Rf_setVar(SEXP symbol, SEXP value, SEXP rho);
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-Rf_005fdefineVar" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fdefineVar-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fsetVar" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fsetVar-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

can be used to assign values to R variables. `Rf_defineVar` creates a new binding or changes the value of an existing binding in the specified environment frame; it is the analogue of `assign(symbol, value, envir = rho, inherits = FALSE)`, but unlike `assign`, `Rf_defineVar` does not make a copy of the object `value`.<a href="#FOOT163" id="DOCF163" class="footnote"><sup>163</sup></a> `Rf_setVar` searches for an existing binding for `symbol` in `rho` or its enclosing environments. If a binding is found, its value is changed to `value`. Otherwise, a new binding with the specified value is created in the global environment. This corresponds to `assign(symbol, value, envir = rho, inherits = TRUE)`.

At times it may also be useful to create a new environment frame in C code. `R_NewEnv` is a C version of the R function `new.env`:

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP R_NewEnv(SEXP enclos, int hash, int size)
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fNewEnv" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fNewEnv-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Some-convenience-functions" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Named-objects-and-copying" rel="next">Named objects and copying</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Finding-and-setting-variables" rel="prev">Finding and setting variables</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.11 Some convenience functions <a href="#Some-convenience-functions-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

Some operations are done so frequently that there are convenience functions to handle them. (All these are provided *via* the header file `Rinternals.h`.)

Suppose we wanted to pass a single logical argument `ignore_quotes`: we could use

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
    int ign = Rf_asLogical(ignore_quotes);
    if(ign == NA_LOGICAL) Rf_error("'ignore_quotes' must be TRUE or FALSE");
```

</div>

which will do any coercion needed (at least from a vector argument), and return `NA_LOGICAL` if the value passed was `NA` or coercion failed. There are also `Rf_asInteger`, `Rf_asReal` and `Rf_asComplex`. The function `Rf_asChar` returns a `CHARSXP`. All of these functions ignore any elements of an input vector after the first.

`Rf_asRboolean` is a stricter version of `Rf_asLogical` introduced in R 4.5.0. It returns type `Rboolean` and gives an error for an input of length other than one, and for coercion failure. `Rf_asBool` is a variant returning the C99/C23/C++ type `bool`.

<span id="index-Rf_005fasInteger" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasInteger-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasLogical" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasLogical-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasReal" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasReal-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasComplex" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasComplex-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasChar" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasChar-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasRboolean" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasRboolean-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasBool" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasBool-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The function `Rf_asCharacterFactor` converts a factor to a character vector. <span id="index-Rf_005fasCharacterFactor" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fasCharacterFactor-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

To return a length-one real vector we can use

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
    double x;

    ...
    return Rf_ScalarReal(x);
```

</div>

and there are versions of this for all the atomic vector types (those for a length-one character vector being `Rf_ScalarString` with argument a `CHARSXP` and `Rf_mkString` with argument `const char *`).

<span id="index-Rf_005fScalarReal" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarReal-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarInteger" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarInteger-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarLogical" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarLogical-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarComplex" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarComplex-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarRaw" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarRaw-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fScalarString-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fmkString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fmkString-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP Rf_ScalarReal(double);
SEXP Rf_ScalarInteger(int);
SEXP Rf_ScalarLogical(int)
SEXP Rf_ScalarRaw(Rbyte);
SEXP Rf_ScalarComplex(Rcomplex);
SEXP Rf_ScalarString(SEXP);
SEXP Rf_mkString(const char *);
```

</div>

</div>

Some useful pre-allocated values are available as `R_BlankScalarString`, `R_BlankString`, and `R_NaString` <span id="index-R_005fBlankScalarString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBlankScalarString-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBlankString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBlankString-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fNaString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fNaString-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

(`Rf_isVectorList`) (with no check on attributes). `Rf_isMatrix` is a test of a length-2 `"dim"` attribute. <span id="index-Rf_005fisVector" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisVector-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisVectorAtomic" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisVectorAtomic-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisVectorList" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisVectorList-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisLanguage" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisLanguage-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisNewList" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisNewList-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisList" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisList-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisOrdered" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisOrdered-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisUnordered" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span Some additional predicates: <span id="index-Rf_005fisBlankString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisBlankString-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisScalarString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisScalarString-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fStringBlank" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fStringBlank-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fStringFalse" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fStringFalse-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fStringTrue" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fStringTrue-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-IS_005fLONG_005fVEC" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-IS_005fLONG_005fVEC-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-IS_005fSCALAR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-IS_005fSCALAR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
Rboolean Rf_isBlankString(const char *);
Rboolean Rf_isScalarString(SEXP);
Rboolean Rf_StringBlank(SEXP);
Rboolean Rf_StringFalse(const char *);
Rboolean Rf_StringTrue(const char *);
int IS_LONG_VEC(SEXP);
int IS_SCALAR(SEXP, int);
```

</div>

</div>

There are a series of small macros/functions to help construct pairlists and language objects (whose internal structures just differ by `SEXPTYPE`). Function `CONS(u, v)` is the basic building block: it constructs a pairlist from `u` followed by `v` (which is a pairlist or `R_NilValue`). `LCONS` is a variant that constructs a language object. #### 5.9.11.1 Semi-internal convenience functions <a href="#Semi_002dinternal-convenience-functions-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

There is quite a collection of functions that may be used in your C code *if* you are willing to adapt to rare API changes. These typically contain the “workhorses” of their R counterparts.

Functions `Rf_any_duplicated` and `Rf_any_duplicated3` are fast versions of R’s `any(duplicated(.))`. <span id="index-Rf_005fany_005fduplicated" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fany_005fduplicated-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fany_005fduplicated3" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fany_005fduplicated3-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Function `R_compute_identical` corresponds to R’s `identical` function. <span id="index-R_005fcompute_005fidentical" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fcompute_005fidentical-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> Function `R_BindingIsLocked` corresponds to R’s `bindingIsLocked` function. Function `R_ParentEnv` corresponds to R’s `parent.env`. <span id="index-R_005fParentEnv" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fParentEnv-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fActiveBindingFunction" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fActiveBindingFunction-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBindingIsActive" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBindingIsActive-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBindingIsLocked" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBindingIsLocked-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fEnvironmentIsLocked" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fEnvironmentIsLocked-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fLockBinding" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fLockBinding-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fLockEnvironment" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fLockEnvironment-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fMakeActiveBinding" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fMakeActiveBinding-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005funLockBinding" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005funLockBinding-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The C functions `Rf_inherits` and `Rf_topenv` correspond to the R functions of the same base name. The C function `Rf_GetOption1` corresponds to the R function `getOption` without specifying a default. <span id="index-Rf_005finherits" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005finherits-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005ftopenv" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005ftopenv-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetOption1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetOption1-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> `Rf_GetOptionWidth` returns the value of the `width` option as an `int`. <span id="index-Rf_005fGetOptionWidth" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fGetOptionWidth-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> The C function `Rf_nlevels` returns the number of levels of a factor. Unlike its R counterpart it always returns zero for non-factors. <span id="index-Rf_005fnlevels" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fnlevels-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

For vectors the C function `Rf_duplicated` returns a logical vector indicating for each element whether it is duplicated or not. A second argument specifies the direction of the search. <span id="index-Rf_005fduplicated" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fduplicated-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Some convenience functions for working with pairlist objects include `Rf_copyListMatrix`, `Rf_listAppend`, `Rf_isVectorizable`, `Rf_VectorToPairList`, and `Rf_PairToVectorList` <span id="index-Rf_005fcopyListMatrix" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcopyListMatrix-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005flistAppend" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005flistAppend-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisVectorizable" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fisVectorizable-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fVectorToPairList" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fVectorToPairList-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fPairToVectorList" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fPairToVectorList-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div id="Named-objects-and-copying" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Resizing-vectors" rel="next">Resizing vectors</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Some-convenience-functions" rel="prev">Some convenience functions</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.12 Named objects and copying <a href="#Named-objects-and-copying-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Copying-objects" class="index-entry-id"></span>

\[The `NAMED` mechanism has been replaced by reference counting.\]

When assignments are done in R such as

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
x <- 1:10
y <- x
```

</div>

the named object is not necessarily copied, so after those two assignments `y` and `x` are bound to the same `SEXPREC` (the structure a `SEXP` points to). This means that any code which alters one of them has to make a copy before modifying the copy if the usual R semantics are to apply. Note that whereas `.C` and `.Fortran` do copy their arguments, `.Call` and `.External` do not. So `Rf_duplicate` is commonly called on arguments to `.Call` before modifying them. If only the top level is modified it may suffice to call `Rf_shallow_duplicate`. <span id="index-Rf_005fduplicate" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fduplicate-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fshallow_005fduplicate" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fshallow_005fduplicate-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

At times it may be necessary to copy attributes from one object to another. This can be done using `DUPLICATE_ATTRIB` or `SHALLOW_DUPLICATE_ATTRIB`. <span id="index-DUPLICATE_005fATTRIB" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-DUPLICATE_005fATTRIB-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SHALLOW_005fDUPLICATE_005fATTRIB" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SHALLOW_005fDUPLICATE_005fATTRIB-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> `ANY_ATTRIB` checks whether there are any attributes, and `CLEAR_ATTRIB` removes all attributes. <span id="index-ANY_005fATTRIB" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-ANY_005fATTRIB-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CLEAR_005fATTRIB" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CLEAR_005fATTRIB-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

However, at least some of this copying is unneeded. In the first assignment shown, `x <- 1:10`, R first creates an object with value `1:10` and then assigns it to `x` but if `x` is modified no copy is necessary as the temporary object with value `1:10` cannot be referred to again. R distinguishes between named and unnamed objects *via* a field in a `SEXPREC` that can be accessed *via* the macros `NAMED` and `SET_NAMED`. This can take values

`0`  
The object is not bound to any symbol

`1`  
The object has been bound to exactly one symbol

`>= 2`  
The object has potentially been bound to two or more symbols, and one should act as if another variable is currently bound to this value. The maximal value is `NAMEDMAX`.

Note the past tenses: R does not do currently do full reference counting and there may currently be fewer bindings.

It is safe to modify the value of any `SEXP` for which `NAMED(foo)` is zero, and if `NAMED(foo)` is two or more, the value should be duplicated (*via* a call to `Rf_duplicate`) before any modification. Note that it is the responsibility of the author of the code making the modification to do the duplication, even if it is `x` whose value is being modified after `y <- x`.

The case `NAMED(foo) == 1` allows some optimization, but it can be ignored (and duplication done whenever `NAMED(foo) > 0`). (This optimization is not currently usable in user code.) It is intended for use within replacement functions. Suppose we used

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
x <- 1:10
foo(x) <- 3
```

</div>

which is computed as

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
x <- 1:10
x <- "foo<-"(x, 3)
```

</div>

Then inside `"foo<-"` the object pointing to the current value of `x` will have `NAMED(foo)` as one, and it would be safe to modify it as the only symbol bound to it is `x` and that will be rebound immediately. (Provided the remaining code in `"foo<-"` make no reference to `x`, and no one is going to attempt a direct call such as `y <- "foo<-"(x)`.)

This mechanism was replaced in R 4.0.0. To support future changes, package code should use `NO_REFERENCES`, `MAYBE_REFERENCED`, `NOT_SHARED`, `MAYBE_SHARED`, and `MARK_NOT_MUTABLE`. <span id="index-NO_005fREFERENCES" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NO_005fREFERENCES-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-MAYBE_005fREFERENCED" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-MAYBE_005fREFERENCED-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NOT_005fSHARED" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NOT_005fSHARED-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-MAYBE_005fSHARED" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-MAYBE_005fSHARED-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-MARK_005fNOT_005fMUTABLE" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-MARK_005fNOT_005fMUTABLE-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Resizing-vectors" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Named-objects-and-copying" rel="prev">Named objects and copying</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="up">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.9.13 Resizing vectors <a href="#Resizing-vectors-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Resizing-vectors" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The functions `Rf_lengthgets` and `Rf_xlengthgets` are analogous to using `length(x) <- n` in R. These functions typically allocate a fresh object. Elements from the original vector are copied into the result up to the specified new length. <span id="index-Rf_005flengthgets" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005flengthgets-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fxlengthgets" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fxlengthgets-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

On rare occasions it may be useful to allocate a longer vector and destructively set its length to a shorter value. This is possible if a vector has been marked as resizable at allocation. An experimental framework to support this has been added in R 4.6.0.

Resizable vectors can be created by an initial allocation or as a copy of an existing vector:

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP R_allocResizableVector(SEXPTYPE type, R_xlen_t maxlen);
SEXP R_duplicateAsResizable(SEXP x);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fallocResizableVector" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fallocResizableVector-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fduplicateAsResizable" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fduplicateAsResizable-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

A resizable vector can then be resized with

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
void R_resizeVector(SEXP x, R_xlen_t newlen);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fresizeVector" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fresizeVector-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

It is an error to attempt to resize a vector that is not resizable, or to request a size greater than the initial allocated size. Resizing a vector will drop `dim`, `dimnames`, and `names` attributes; other attributes are retained.

Whether a vector is resizable and the maximal available size of a resizable vector can be determined using

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
bool R_isResizable(SEXP x);
R_xlen_t R_maxLength(SEXP x);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fisResizable" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fisResizable-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fmaxLength" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fmaxLength-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Some considerations for using resizable vectors:

- Resizing a vector is a destructive modification. Like any destructive modification at the `C` level it has to be done with care to avoid violating the pass-by-value semantics of the `R` language. Ordinarily only objects with no references are safe to modify; if an object has references from other R objects then these must be thoroughly understood before considering a destructive modification.
- If enabling package code to resize vectors that have references causes too many issues, then `R_resizeVector` may be modified to disallow this.
- Serializing and unserializing a resizable vector does not preserve the resizable property. The result is an ordinary non-resizable vector.
- The memory between a shorter length and the initially allocated maximal length of a resizable vector is not accessible and cannot be reclaimed until the shorter vector is reclaimed by the garbage collector.

In most cases using `Rf_lengthgets` or `Rf_xlengthgets` is a better, safer, and more memory-efficient choice than using resizable vectors.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

</div>
