<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Evaluating-R-expressions-from-C" rel="next">Evaluating R expressions from C</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Handling-R-objects-in-C" rel="prev">Handling R objects in C</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#System-and-foreign-language-interfaces" rel="up">System and foreign language interfaces</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

### 5.10 Interface functions `.Call` and `.External` <a href="#Interface-functions-_002eCall-and-_002eExternal-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Interfaces-to-compiled-code-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

In this section we consider the details of the R/C interfaces.

These two interfaces have almost the same functionality. `.Call` is based on the interface of the same name in S version 4, and `.External` is based on R’s `.Internal`. `.External` is more complex but allows a variable number of arguments.

- [Calling `.Call`](#Calling-_002eCall)
- [Calling `.External`](#Calling-_002eExternal)
- [Missing and special values](#Missing-and-special-values)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<div id="Calling-_002eCall" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Calling-_002eExternal" rel="next">Calling <code class="code">.External</code></a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Interface-functions-_002eCall-and-_002eExternal" rel="up">Interface functions <code class="code">.Call</code> and <code class="code">.External</code></a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.10.1 Calling `.Call` <a href="#Calling-_002eCall-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-_002eCall-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Let us convert our finite convolution example to use `.Call`. The calling function in R is

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
conv <- function(a, b) .Call("convolve2", a, b)
```

</div>

which could hardly be simpler, but as we shall see all the type coercion is transferred to the C code, which is

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

SEXP convolve2(SEXP a, SEXP b)
{
    int na, nb, nab;
    double *xa, *xb, *xab;
    SEXP ab;

    a = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(a, REALSXP));
    b = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(b, REALSXP));
    na = Rf_length(a); nb = Rf_length(b); nab = na + nb - 1;
    ab = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, nab));
    xa = REAL(a); xb = REAL(b); xab = REAL(ab);
    for(int i = 0; i < nab; i++) xab[i] = 0.0;
    for(int i = 0; i < na; i++)
        for(int j = 0; j < nb; j++) xab[i + j] += xa[i] * xb[j];
    UNPROTECT(3);
    return ab;
}
```

</div>

</div>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Calling-_002eExternal" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Missing-and-special-values" rel="next">Missing and special values</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Calling-_002eCall" rel="prev">Calling <code class="code">.Call</code></a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Interface-functions-_002eCall-and-_002eExternal" rel="up">Interface functions <code class="code">.Call</code> and <code class="code">.External</code></a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.10.2 Calling `.External` <a href="#Calling-_002eExternal-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-_002eExternal-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

We can use the same example to illustrate `.External`. The R code changes only by replacing `.Call` by `.External`

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
conv <- function(a, b) .External("convolveE", a, b)
```

</div>

but the main change is how the arguments are passed to the C code, this time as a single SEXP. The only change to the C code is how we handle the arguments.

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>

SEXP convolveE(SEXP args)
{
    int i, j, na, nb, nab;
    double *xa, *xb, *xab;
    SEXP a, b, ab;

    a = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(CADR(args), REALSXP));
    b = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(CADDR(args), REALSXP));
    ...
}
```

</div>

</div>

Once again we do not need to protect the arguments, as in the R side of the interface they are objects that are already in use. The macros

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
  first = CADR(args);
  second = CADDR(args);
  third = CADDDR(args);
  fourth = CAD4R(args);
  fifth  = CAD5R(args);
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-CADR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CADR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CADDR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CADDR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CADDDR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CADDDR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CAD4R" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CAD4R-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CAD5R" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CAD5R-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

provide convenient ways to access the first five arguments. More generally we can use the <span id="index-CAR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CAR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CDR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CDR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> `CDR` and `CAR` macros as in

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
  args = CDR(args); a = CAR(args);
  args = CDR(args); b = CAR(args);
```

</div>

</div>

which clearly allows us to extract an unlimited number of arguments (whereas `.Call` has a limit, albeit at 65 not a small one).

More usefully, the `.External` interface provides an easy way to handle calls with a variable number of arguments, as `length(args)` will give the number of arguments supplied (of which the first is ignored). We may need to know the names (‘tags’) given to the actual arguments, which we can by using the `TAG` macro and using something like the following example, that prints the names and the first value of its arguments if they are vector types.

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP showArgs(SEXP args)
{
    void *vmax = vmaxget();
    args = CDR(args); /* skip 'name' */
    for(int i = 0; args != R_NilValue; i++, args = CDR(args)) {
        const char *name =
            Rf_isNull(TAG(args)) ? "" : Rf_translateChar(PRINTNAME(TAG(args)));
        SEXP el = CAR(args);
        if (length(el) == 0) {
            Rprintf("[%d] '%s' R type, length 0\n", i+1, name);
           continue;
        }
```

</div>

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
        switch(TYPEOF(el)) {
        case REALSXP:
            Rprintf("[%d] '%s' %f\n", i+1, name, REAL(el)[0]);
            break;
```

</div>

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
        case LGLSXP:
        case INTSXP:
            Rprintf("[%d] '%s' %d\n", i+1, name, INTEGER(el)[0]);
            break;
```

</div>

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
        case CPLXSXP:
        {
            Rcomplex cpl = COMPLEX(el)[0];
            Rprintf("[%d] '%s' %f + %fi\n", i+1, name, cpl.r, cpl.i);
        }
            break;
```

</div>

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
        case STRSXP:
            Rprintf("[%d] '%s' %s\n", i+1, name,
                   Rf_translateChar(STRING_ELT(el, 0)));
           break;
```

</div>

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
        default:
            Rprintf("[%d] '%s' R type\n", i+1, name);
       }
    }
    vmaxset(vmax);
    return R_NilValue;
}
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-PRINTNAME" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-PRINTNAME-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-TYPEOF" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-TYPEOF-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-TAG" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-TAG-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

This can be called by the wrapper function

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
showArgs <- function(...) invisible(.External("showArgs", ...))
```

</div>

Note that this style of programming is convenient but not necessary, as an alternative style is

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
showArgs1 <- function(...) invisible(.Call("showArgs1", list(...)))
```

</div>

The (very similar) C code is in the scripts.

Additional functions for accessing pairlist components are `CAAR`, `CDAR`, `CDDR`, and `CDDDR`. <span id="index-CAAR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CAAR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CDAR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CDAR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CDDR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CDDR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CDDDR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CDDDR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> These components can be modified with `SETCAR`, `SETCDR`, `SETCADR`, `SETCADDR`, `SETCADDDR`, and `SETCAD4R`. <span id="index-SETCAR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCAR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCDR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCDR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCADR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCADR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCADDR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCADDR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCADDDR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCADDDR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCAD4R" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SETCAD4R-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Missing-and-special-values" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Calling-_002eExternal" rel="prev">Calling <code class="code">.External</code></a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Interface-functions-_002eCall-and-_002eExternal" rel="up">Interface functions <code class="code">.Call</code> and <code class="code">.External</code></a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.10.3 Missing and special values <a href="#Missing-and-special-values-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Missing-values" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-IEEE-special-values" class="index-entry-id"></span>

One piece of error-checking the `.C` call does (unless `NAOK` is true) is to check for missing (`NA`) and <span class="abbr acronym">IEEE</span> special values (`Inf`, `-Inf` and `NaN`) and give an error if any are found. With the `.Call` interface these will be passed to our code. In this example the special values are no problem, as <span class="abbr acronym">IEC</span> 60559 arithmetic will handle them correctly. In the current implementation this is also true of `NA` as it is a type of `NaN`, but it is unwise to rely on such details. Thus we will re-write the code to handle `NA`s using macros defined in `R_ext/Arith.h` included by `R.h`. <span id="index-R_005fext_002fArith_002eh" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fisnancpp" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fisnancpp-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The code changes are the same in any of the versions of `convolve2` or `convolveE`:

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    ...
  for(int i = 0; i < na; i++)
    for(int j = 0; j < nb; j++)
        if(ISNA(xa[i]) || ISNA(xb[j]) || ISNA(xab[i + j]))
            xab[i + j] = NA_REAL;
        else
            xab[i + j] += xa[i] * xb[j];
    ...
```

</div>

</div>

<span id="index-ISNA" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-ISNA-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-ISNAN" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-ISNAN-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NA_005fREAL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NA_005fREAL-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NA_005fLOGICAL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NA_005fLOGICAL-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NA_005fINTEGER" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NA_005fINTEGER-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NA_005fSTRING" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-NA_005fSTRING-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Note that the `ISNA` macro, and the similar macros `ISNAN` (which checks for `NaN` or `NA`) and `R_FINITE` (which is false for `NA` and all the special values), only apply to numeric values of type `double`. Missingness of integers, logicals and character strings can be tested by equality to the constants `NA_INTEGER`, `NA_LOGICAL` and `NA_STRING`. These and `NA_REAL` can be used to set elements of R vectors to `NA`.

The constants `R_NaN`, `R_PosInf` and `R_NegInf` can be used to set `double`s to the special values.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

</div>

<div id="Evaluating-R-expressions-from-C" class="section-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Parsing-R-code-from-C" rel="next">Parsing R code from C</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Interface-functions-_002eCall-and-_002eExternal" rel="prev">Interface functions <code class="code">.Call</code> and <code class="code">.External</code></a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#System-and-foreign-language-interfaces" rel="up">System and foreign language interfaces</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

### 5.11 Evaluating R expressions from C <a href="#Evaluating-R-expressions-from-C-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Evaluating-R-expressions-from-C" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The main function we will use is

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP Rf_eval(SEXP expr, SEXP rho);
```

</div>

<span id="index-Rf_005feval" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005feval-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

the equivalent of the interpreted R code `eval(expr, envir = rho)` (so `rho` must be an environment), although we can also make use of `R_getVar`, `Rf_defineVar` and `Rf_findFun` (which restricts the search to functions). <span id="index-Rf_005ffindFun" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005ffindFun-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

To see how this might be applied, here is a simplified internal version of `lapply` for expressions, used as

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
a <- list(a = 1:5, b = rnorm(10), test = runif(100))
.Call("lapply", a, quote(sum(x)), new.env())
```

</div>

</div>

with C code

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP lapply(SEXP list, SEXP expr, SEXP rho)
{
    int n = Rf_length(list);
    SEXP ans;

    if(!Rf_isNewList(list)) Rf_error("'list' must be a list");
    if(!Rf_isEnvironment(rho)) Rf_error("'rho' should be an environment");
    ans = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(VECSXP, n));
    for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        Rf_defineVar(Rf_install("x"), VECTOR_ELT(list, i), rho);
        SET_VECTOR_ELT(ans, i, Rf_eval(expr, rho));
    }
    Rf_setAttrib(ans, R_NamesSymbol, Rf_getAttrib(list, R_NamesSymbol));
    UNPROTECT(1);
    return ans;
}
```

</div>

</div>

It would be closer to `lapply` if we could pass in a function rather than an expression. One way to do this is *via* interpreted R code as in the next example, but it is possible (if somewhat obscure) to do this in C code. The following is based on the code in `src/main/optimize.c`.

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP lapply2(SEXP list, SEXP fn, SEXP rho)
{
    int n = length(list);
    SEXP R_fcall, ans;

    if(!Rf_isNewList(list)) Rf_error("'list' must be a list");
    if(!Rf_isFunction(fn)) Rf_error("'fn' must be a function");
    if(!Rf_isEnvironment(rho)) Rf_error("'rho' should be an environment");
    R_fcall = PROTECT(Rf_lang2(fn, R_NilValue));
    ans = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(VECSXP, n));
    for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        SETCADR(R_fcall, VECTOR_ELT(list, i));
        SET_VECTOR_ELT(ans, i, Rf_eval(R_fcall, rho));
    }
    Rf_setAttrib(ans, R_NamesSymbol, Rf_getAttrib(list, R_NamesSymbol));
    UNPROTECT(2);
    return ans;
}
```

</div>

</div>

used by

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
.Call("lapply2", a, sum, new.env())
```

</div>

Function `Rf_lang2` creates an executable pairlist of two elements, but this will only be clear to those with a knowledge of a LISP-like language.

As a more comprehensive example of constructing an R call in C code and evaluating, consider the following fragment. Similar code appears in the definition of `do_docall` in `src/main/coerce.c`.

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
    SEXP s, t;
    t = s = PROTECT(Rf_allocLang(3));
    SETCAR(t, Rf_install("print")); t = CDR(t);
    SETCAR(t,  CAR(a)); t = CDR(t);
    SETCAR(t, Rf_ScalarInteger(digits));
    SET_TAG(t, Rf_install("digits"));
    Rf_eval(s, env);
    UNPROTECT(1);
```

</div>

<span id="index-Rf_005fallocLang" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocLang-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fTAG" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fTAG-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The function `Rf_allocLang` is available as of R 4.4.1; for older versions replace `Rf_allocLang(3)` with

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
LCONS(R_NilValue, Rf_allocList(2))
```

</div>

<span id="index-LCONS-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LCONS-3" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocList-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocList-3" class="index-entry-id"></span>

At this point `CAR(a)` is the R object to be printed, the current attribute. There are three steps: the call is constructed as a pairlist of length 3, the list is filled in, and the expression represented by the pairlist is evaluated.

A pairlist is quite distinct from a generic vector list, the only user-visible form of list in R. A pairlist is a linked list (with `CDR(t)` computing the next entry), with items (accessed by `CAR(t)`) and names or tags (set by `SET_TAG`). In this call there are to be three items, a symbol (pointing to the function to be called) and two argument values, the first unnamed and the second named. Setting the type to `LANGSXP` makes this a call which can be evaluated.

Customarily, the evaluation environment is passed from the calling R code (see `rho` above). In special cases it is possible that the C code may need to obtain the current evaluation environment which can be done via `R_GetCurrentEnv()` function. This function is experimental and may be changed or removed in the future. <span id="index-R_005fGetCurrentEnv" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fGetCurrentEnv-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

- [Zero-finding](#Zero_002dfinding)
- [Calculating numerical derivatives](#Calculating-numerical-derivatives)

#### 5.11.1 Zero-finding <a href="#Zero_002dfinding-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Zero_002dfinding" class="index-entry-id"></span>

In this section we re-work the example of Becker, Chambers & Wilks (1988, pp.~205–10) on finding a zero of a univariate function. The R code and an example are

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
zero <- function(f, guesses, tol = 1e-7) {
    f.check <- function(x) {
        x <- f(x)
        if(!is.numeric(x)) stop("Need a numeric result")
        as.double(x)
    }
    .Call("zero", body(f.check), as.double(guesses), as.double(tol),
          new.env())
}

cube1 <- function(x) (x^2 + 1) * (x - 1.5)
zero(cube1, c(0, 5))
```

</div>

where this time we do the coercion and error-checking in the R code. The C code is

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP mkans(double x)
{
    // no need for PROTECT() here, as REAL(.) does not allocate:
    SEXP ans = Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, 1);
    REAL(ans)[0] = x;
    return ans;
}
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted

```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
double feval(double x, SEXP f, SEXP rho)
{
    // a version with (too) much PROTECT()ion .. "better safe than sorry"
    SEXP symbol, value;
    PROTECT(symbol = Rf_install("x"));
    PROTECT(value = mkans(x));
    Rf_defineVar(symbol, value, rho);
    UNPROTECT(2);
    return(REAL(Rf_eval(f, rho))[0]);
}
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted

```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP zero(SEXP f, SEXP guesses, SEXP stol, SEXP rho)
{
    double x0 = REAL(guesses)[0], x1 = REAL(guesses)[1],
           tol = REAL(stol)[0];
    double f0, f1, fc, xc;
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted

```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    if(tol <= 0.0) Rf_error("non-positive tol value");
    f0 = feval(x0, f, rho); f1 = feval(x1, f, rho);
    if(f0 == 0.0) return mkans(x0);
    if(f1 == 0.0) return mkans(x1);
    if(f0*f1 > 0.0) error("x[0] and x[1] have the same sign");
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted

```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    for(;;) {
        xc = 0.5*(x0+x1);
        if(fabs(x0-x1) < tol) return  mkans(xc);
        fc = feval(xc, f, rho);
        if(fc == 0) return  mkans(xc);
        if(f0*fc > 0.0) {
            x0 = xc; f0 = fc;
        } else {
            x1 = xc; f1 = fc;
        }
    }
}
```

</div>

</div>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Calculating-numerical-derivatives" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Zero_002dfinding" rel="prev">Zero-finding</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Evaluating-R-expressions-from-C" rel="up">Evaluating R expressions from C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.11.2 Calculating numerical derivatives <a href="#Calculating-numerical-derivatives-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Numerical-derivatives" class="index-entry-id"></span>

We will use a longer example (by Saikat DebRoy) to illustrate the use of evaluation and `.External`. This calculates numerical derivatives, something that could be done as effectively in interpreted R code but may be needed as part of a larger C calculation.

An interpreted R version and an example are

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
numeric.deriv <- function(expr, theta, rho=sys.frame(sys.parent()))
{
    eps <- sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)
    ans <- eval(substitute(expr), rho)
    grad <- matrix(, length(ans), length(theta),
                   dimnames=list(NULL, theta))
    for (i in seq_along(theta)) {
        old <- get(theta[i], envir=rho)
        delta <- eps * max(1, abs(old))
        assign(theta[i], old+delta, envir=rho)
        ans1 <- eval(substitute(expr), rho)
        assign(theta[i], old, envir=rho)
        grad[, i] <- (ans1 - ans)/delta
    }
    attr(ans, "gradient") <- grad
    ans
}
omega <- 1:5; x <- 1; y <- 2
numeric.deriv(sin(omega*x*y), c("x", "y"))
```

</div>

</div>

where `expr` is an expression, `theta` a character vector of variable names and `rho` the environment to be used.

For the compiled version the call from R will be

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
.External("numeric_deriv", expr, theta, rho)
```

</div>

with example usage

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
.External("numeric_deriv", quote(sin(omega*x*y)),
          c("x", "y"), .GlobalEnv)
```

</div>

Note the need to quote the expression to stop it being evaluated in the caller.

Here is the complete C code which we will explain section by section.

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include <float.h> /* for DBL_EPSILON */

SEXP numeric_deriv(SEXP args)
{
    SEXP theta, expr, rho, ans, ans1, gradient, par, dimnames;
    double tt, xx, delta, eps = sqrt(DBL_EPSILON), *rgr, *rans;
    int i, start;
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted

```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    expr = CADR(args);
    if(!Rf_isString(theta = CADDR(args)))
        Rf_error("theta should be of type character");
    if(!Rf_isEnvironment(rho = CADDDR(args)))
        Rf_error("rho should be an environment");
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted

```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    ans = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(eval(expr, rho), REALSXP));
    gradient = PROTECT(Rf_allocMatrix(REALSXP, LENGTH(ans), LENGTH(theta)));
    rgr = REAL(gradient); rans = REAL(ans);
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted
```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    for(i = 0, start = 0; i < LENGTH(theta); i++, start += LENGTH(ans)) {
        par = PROTECT(R_getVar(Rf_installChar(STRING_ELT(theta, i)), rho, TRUE));
        tt = REAL(par)[0];
        xx = fabs(tt);
        delta = (xx < 1) ? eps : xx*eps;
        REAL(par)[0] += delta;
        ans1 = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(Rf_eval(expr, rho), REALSXP));
        for(int j = 0; j < LENGTH(ans); j++)
            rgr[j + start] = (REAL(ans1)[j] - rans[j])/delta;
        REAL(par)[0] = tt;
        UNPROTECT(2); /* par, ans1 */
    }
```

</div>

``` example-preformatted

```

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    dimnames = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(VECSXP, 2));
    SET_VECTOR_ELT(dimnames, 1,  theta);
    Rf_dimnamesgets(gradient, dimnames);
    Rf_setAttrib(ans, Rf_install("gradient"), gradient);
    UNPROTECT(3); /* ans  gradient  dimnames */
    return ans;
}
```

</div>

</div>

The code to handle the arguments is

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    expr = CADR(args);
    if(!Rf_isString(theta = CADDR(args)))
        Rf_error("theta should be of type character");
    if(!Rf_isEnvironment(rho = CADDDR(args)))
        Rf_error("rho should be an environment");
```

</div>

</div>

Note that we check for correct types of `theta` and `rho` but do not check the type of `expr`. That is because `eval` can handle many types of R objects other than `EXPRSXP`. There is no useful coercion we can do, so we stop with an error message if the arguments are not of the correct mode.

The first step in the code is to evaluate the expression in the environment `rho`, by

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
    ans = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(eval(expr, rho), REALSXP));
```

</div>

We then allocate space for the calculated derivative by

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
    gradient = PROTECT(Rf_allocMatrix(REALSXP, LENGTH(ans), LENGTH(theta)));
```

</div>

The first argument to `Rf_allocMatrix` gives the `SEXPTYPE` of the matrix: here we want it to be `REALSXP`. The other two arguments are the numbers of rows and columns. (Note that `LENGTH` is intended to be used for vectors: `Rf_length` is more generally applicable.) <span id="index-Rf_005fallocMatrix-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fallocMatrix-3" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    for(i = 0, start = 0; i < LENGTH(theta); i++, start += LENGTH(ans)) {
        par = PROTECT(R_getVar(Rf_installChar(STRING_ELT(theta, i)), rho, TRUE));
```

</div>

</div>

Here, we are entering a for loop. We loop through each of the variables. In the `for` loop, we first create a symbol corresponding to the `i`-th element of the `STRSXP` `theta`. Here, `STRING_ELT(theta, i)` accesses the `i`-th element of the `STRSXP` `theta`. `installChar()` installs the element as a name and `R_getVar` finds its value in `rho`. <span id="index-CHAR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-CHAR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fCHAR" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fCHAR-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
        tt = REAL(par)[0];
        xx = fabs(tt);
        delta = (xx < 1) ? eps : xx*eps;
        REAL(par)[0] += delta;
        ans1 = PROTECT(Rf_coerceVector(eval(expr, rho), REALSXP));
```

</div>

</div>

We first extract the real value of the parameter, then calculate `delta`, the increment to be used for approximating the numerical derivative. Then we change the value stored in `par` (in environment `rho`) by `delta` and evaluate `expr` in environment `rho` again. Because we are directly dealing with original R memory locations here, R does the evaluation for the changed parameter value.

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
        for(int j = 0; j < LENGTH(ans); j++)
            rgr[j + start] = (REAL(ans1)[j] - rans[j])/delta;
        REAL(par)[0] = tt;
        UNPROTECT(2);
    }
```

</div>

</div>

Now, we compute the `i`-th column of the gradient matrix. Note how it is accessed: R stores matrices by column (like Fortran).

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
    dimnames = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(VECSXP, 2));
    SET_VECTOR_ELT(dimnames, 1, theta);
    Rf_dimnamesgets(gradient, dimnames);
    Rf_setAttrib(ans, install("gradient"), gradient);
    UNPROTECT(3);
    return ans;
}
```

</div>

</div>

First we add column names to the gradient matrix. This is done by allocating a list (a `VECSXP`) whose first element, the row names, is `NULL` (the default) and the second element, the column names, is set as `theta`. This list is then assigned as the attribute having the symbol `R_DimNamesSymbol`. Finally we set the gradient matrix as the gradient attribute of `ans`, unprotect the remaining protected locations and return the answer `ans`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

</div>

### 5.12 Parsing R code from C <a href="#Parsing-R-code-from-C-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Parsing-R-code-from-C" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Suppose an R extension wants to accept an R expression from the user and evaluate it. The previous section covered evaluation, but the expression will be entered as text and needs to be parsed first. A small part of R’s parse interface is declared in header file `R_ext/Parse.h`<a href="#FOOT164" id="DOCF164" class="footnote"><sup>164</sup></a>.

An example of the usage can be found in the (example) Windows package **windlgs** included in the R source tree. The essential part is

<div class="example">

<div class="group">

``` example-preformatted
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include <R_ext/Parse.h>

SEXP menu_ttest3()
{
    char cmd[256];
    SEXP cmdSexp, cmdexpr, ans = R_NilValue;
    ParseStatus status;
   ...
    if(done == 1) {
        cmdSexp = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(STRSXP, 1));
        SET_STRING_ELT(cmdSexp, 0, Rf_mkChar(cmd));
        cmdexpr = PROTECT(R_ParseVector(cmdSexp, -1, &status, R_NilValue));
        if (status != PARSE_OK) {
            UNPROTECT(2);
            Rf_error("invalid call %s", cmd);
        }
        /* Loop is needed here as EXPSEXP will be of length > 1 */
        for(int i = 0; i < Rf_length(cmdexpr); i++)
            ans = Rf_eval(VECTOR_ELT(cmdexpr, i), R_GlobalEnv);
        UNPROTECT(2);
    }
    return ans;
}
```

</div>

</div>

Note that a single line of text may give rise to more than one R expression. `R_GlobalEnv` provides access from C to the R-level `.GlobalEnv`. The base environment, base namespace, and empty environment can be accessed as `R_BaseEnv`, `R_BaseNamespace`, and `R_EmptyEnv`. <span id="index-R_005fGlobalEnv" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fGlobalEnv-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBaseEnv" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBaseEnv-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBaseNamespace" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fBaseNamespace-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fEmptyEnv" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fEmptyEnv-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<span id="index-R_005fParseVector" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fParseVector-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

`R_ParseVector` is essentially the code used to implement `parse(text=)` at R level. The first argument is a character vector (corresponding to `text`) and the second the maximal number of expressions to parse (corresponding to `n`). The third argument is a pointer to a variable of an enumeration type, and it is normal (as `parse` does) to regard all values other than `PARSE_OK` as an error. Other values which might be returned are `PARSE_INCOMPLETE` (an incomplete expression was found) and `PARSE_ERROR` (a syntax error), in both cases the value returned being `R_NilValue`. The fourth argument is a length one character vector to be used as a filename in error messages, a `srcfile` object or the R `NULL` object (as in the example above). If a `srcfile` object was used, a `srcref` attribute would be attached to the result, containing a list of `srcref` objects of the same length as the expression, to allow it to be echoed with its original formatting.

Two higher-level alternatives are `R_ParseString` and `R_ParseEvalString`:

<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`SEXP` **R_ParseString** `(const char *``str``)` <a href="#index-R_005fParseString-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`SEXP` **R_ParseEvalString** `(const char *``str``, SEXP ``env``)` <a href="#index-R_005fParseEvalString-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
`R_ParseString` Parses the code in `str` and returns the resulting expression. An error is signaled if parsing `str` produces more than one R expression. `R_ParseEvalString ` first parses `str`, then evaluates the expression in the environment `env`, and returns the result.

<span id="index-R_005fParseString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fParseString-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fParseEvalString" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fParseEvalString-2" class="index-entry-id"></span>

An example from `src/main/objects.c`:

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
call = R_ParseString("base::nameOfClass(X)");
```

</div>

- [Accessing source references](#Accessing-source-references)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<div id="Accessing-source-references" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Parsing-R-code-from-C" rel="up">Parsing R code from C</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.12.1 Accessing source references <a href="#Accessing-source-references-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The source references added by the parser are recorded by R’s evaluator as it evaluates code. Two functions make these available to debuggers running C code: <span id="index-R_005fGetCurrentSrcref" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fGetCurrentSrcref-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fGetSrcFilename" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fGetSrcFilename-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP R_GetCurrentSrcref(int skip);
```

</div>

This function checks the current evaluation stack for entries that contain source reference information. There are two modes of operation. If `skip == NA_INTEGER`, the `R_Srcref` entry is checked followed by entries in the call stack, until a `srcref` is found. Otherwise, the `skip` argument tells how many calls to skip (counting from the top of the stack) before returning the `SEXP` of the call’s `srcref` object or `NULL` if that call did not have one. If `skip < 0`, `abs(skip)` locations are counted up from the bottom of the stack. If too few or no source references are found, `NULL` is returned. <span id="index-R_005fSrcref" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fSrcref-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP R_GetSrcFilename(SEXP srcref);
```

</div>

This function extracts the filename from the source reference for display, returning a length 1 character vector containing the filename. If no name is found, `""` is returned.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

</div>

<div id="External-pointers-and-weak-references" class="section-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Vector-accessor-functions" rel="next">Vector accessor functions</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Parsing-R-code-from-C" rel="prev">Parsing R code from C</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#System-and-foreign-language-interfaces" rel="up">System and foreign language interfaces</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

### 5.13 External pointers and weak references <a href="#External-pointers-and-weak-references-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The `SEXPTYPE`s `EXTPTRSXP` and `WEAKREFSXP` can be encountered at R level, but are created in C code.

<span id="index-external-pointer" class="index-entry-id"></span>

External pointer `SEXP`s are intended to handle references to C structures such as ‘handles’, and are used for this purpose in package <a href="https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RODBC" class="url"><strong>RODBC</strong></a> for example. They are unusual in their copying semantics in that when an R object is copied, the external pointer object is not duplicated. (For this reason external pointers should only be used as part of an object with normal semantics, for example an attribute or an element of a list.)

An external pointer is created by

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP R_MakeExternalPtr(void *p, SEXP tag, SEXP prot);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fMakeExternalPtr" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fMakeExternalPtr-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

where `p` is the pointer (and hence this cannot portably be a function pointer), and `tag` and `prot` are references to ordinary R objects which will remain in existence (be protected from garbage collection) for the lifetime of the external pointer object. A useful convention is to use the `tag` field for some form of type identification and the `prot` field for protecting the memory that the external pointer represents, if that memory is allocated from the R heap. Both `tag` and `prot` can be `R_NilValue`, and often are.

An alternative way to create an external pointer from a function pointer is

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
typedef void * (*R_DL_FUNC)();
SEXP R_MakeExternalPtrFn(R_DL_FUNC p, SEXP tag, SEXP prot);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fMakeExternalPtrFn" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fMakeExternalPtrFn-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The elements of an external pointer can be accessed and set *via*

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
void *R_ExternalPtrAddr(SEXP s);
DL_FUNC R_ExternalPtrAddrFn(SEXP s);
SEXP R_ExternalPtrTag(SEXP s);
SEXP R_ExternalPtrProtected(SEXP s);
void R_ClearExternalPtr(SEXP s);
void R_SetExternalPtrAddr(SEXP s, void *p);
void R_SetExternalPtrTag(SEXP s, SEXP tag);
void R_SetExternalPtrProtected(SEXP s, SEXP p);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fExternalPtrAddr" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fExternalPtrAddr-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fExternalPtrAddrFn" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fExternalPtrAddrFn-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fExternalPtrTag" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fExternalPtrTag-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fExternalPtrProtected" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fExternalPtrProtected-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fClearExternalPtr" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fClearExternalPtr-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fSetExternalPtrAddr" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fSetExternalPtrAddr-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fSetExternalPtrTag" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fSetExternalPtrTag-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fSetExternalPtrProtected" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fSetExternalPtrProtected-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Clearing a pointer sets its value to the C `NULL` pointer.

<span id="index-finalizer" class="index-entry-id"></span>

An external pointer object can have a *finalizer*, a piece of code to be run when the object is garbage collected. This can be R code or C code, and the various interfaces are, respectively.

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
void R_RegisterFinalizer(SEXP s, SEXP fun);
void R_RegisterFinalizerEx(SEXP s, SEXP fun, Rboolean onexit);

typedef void (*R_CFinalizer_t)(SEXP);
void R_RegisterCFinalizer(SEXP s, R_CFinalizer_t fun);
void R_RegisterCFinalizerEx(SEXP s, R_CFinalizer_t fun, Rboolean onexit);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fRegisterFinalizer" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fRegisterFinalizer-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fRegisterCFinalizer" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fRegisterCFinalizer-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fRegisterFinalizerEx" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fRegisterFinalizerEx-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fRegisterCFinalizerEx" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fRegisterCFinalizerEx-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

The R function indicated by `fun` should be a function of a single argument, the object to be finalized. R does not perform a garbage collection when shutting down, and the `onexit` argument of the extended forms can be used to ask that the finalizer be run during a normal shutdown of the R session. It is suggested that it is good practice to clear the pointer on finalization.

The only R level function for interacting with external pointers is `reg.finalizer` which can be used to set a finalizer.

It is probably not a good idea to allow an external pointer to be `save`d and then reloaded, but if this happens the pointer will be set to the C `NULL` pointer.

Finalizers can be run at many places in the code base and much of it, including the R interpreter, is not re-entrant. So great care is needed in choosing the code to be run in a finalizer. Finalizers are marked to be run at garbage collection but only run at a somewhat safe point thereafter.

<span id="index-weak-reference" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Weak references are used to allow the programmer to maintain information on entities without preventing the garbage collection of the entities once they become unreachable.

A weak reference contains a key and a value. The value is reachable if it is either reachable directly or *via* weak references with reachable keys. Once a value is determined to be unreachable during garbage collection, the key and value are set to `R_NilValue` and the finalizer will be run later in the garbage collection.

Weak reference objects are created by one of

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP R_MakeWeakRef(SEXP key, SEXP val, SEXP fin, Rboolean onexit);
SEXP R_MakeWeakRefC(SEXP key, SEXP val, R_CFinalizer_t fin,
                    Rboolean onexit);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fMakeWeakRef" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fMakeWeakRef-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fMakeWeakRefC" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fMakeWeakRefC-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

where the R or C finalizer are specified in exactly the same way as for an external pointer object (whose finalization interface is implemented *via* weak references).

The parts can be accessed *via*

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP R_WeakRefKey(SEXP w);
SEXP R_WeakRefValue(SEXP w);
void R_RunWeakRefFinalizer(SEXP w);
```

</div>

<span id="index-R_005fWeakRefKey" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fWeakRefKey-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fWeakRefValue" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fWeakRefValue-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fRunWeakRefFinalizer" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fRunWeakRefFinalizer-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

A toy example of the use of weak references can be found at <a href="https://homepage.stat.uiowa.edu/~luke/R/references/weakfinex.html" class="uref">https://homepage.stat.uiowa.edu/~luke/R/references/weakfinex.html</a>, but that is used to add finalizers to external pointers which can now be done more directly. At the time of writing no <span class="abbr acronym">CRAN</span> or Bioconductor package used weak references.

- [An example](#An-external-pointer-example)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<div id="An-external-pointer-example" class="subsection-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#External-pointers-and-weak-references" rel="up">External pointers and weak references</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

#### 5.13.1 An example <a href="#An-example-2" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

Package <a href="https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RODBC" class="url"><strong>RODBC</strong></a> uses external pointers to maintain its *channels*, connections to databases. There can be several connections open at once, and the status information for each is stored in a C structure (pointed to by `thisHandle` in the code extract below) that is returned *via* an external pointer as part of the **RODBC** ‘channel’ (as the `"handle_ptr"` attribute). The external pointer is created by

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
    SEXP ans, ptr;
    ans = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(INTSXP, 1));
    ptr = R_MakeExternalPtr(thisHandle, Rf_install("RODBC_channel"), R_NilValue);
    PROTECT(ptr);
    R_RegisterCFinalizerEx(ptr, chanFinalizer, TRUE);
            ...
    /* return the channel no */
    INTEGER(ans)[0] = nChannels;
    /* and the connection string as an attribute */
    Rf_setAttrib(ans, Rf_install("connection.string"), constr);
    Rf_setAttrib(ans, Rf_install("handle_ptr"), ptr);
    UNPROTECT(3);
    return ans;
```

</div>

Note the symbol given to identify the usage of the external pointer, and the use of the finalizer. Since the final argument when registering the finalizer is `TRUE`, the finalizer will be run at the end of the R session (unless it crashes). This is used to close and clean up the connection to the database. The finalizer code is simply

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
static void chanFinalizer(SEXP ptr)
{
    if(!R_ExternalPtrAddr(ptr)) return;
    inRODBCClose(R_ExternalPtrAddr(ptr));
    R_ClearExternalPtr(ptr); /* not really needed */
}
```

</div>

Clearing the pointer and checking for a `NULL` pointer avoids any possibility of attempting to close an already-closed channel.

R’s connections provide another example of using external pointers, in that case purely to be able to use a finalizer to close and destroy the connection if it is no longer is use.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

</div>

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Character-encoding-issues" rel="next">Character encoding issues</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#External-pointers-and-weak-references" rel="prev">External pointers and weak references</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#System-and-foreign-language-interfaces" rel="up">System and foreign language interfaces</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

### 5.14 Vector accessor functions <a href="#Vector-accessor-functions-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

The vector accessors like `REAL`, `INTEGER`, `LOGICAL`, `RAW`, `COMPLEX`, and `VECTOR_ELT` are *functions* when used in R extensions. (For efficiency they may be macros or inline functions when used in the R source code, apart from `SET_STRING_ELT` and `SET_VECTOR_ELT` which are always functions. When used outside the R source code all vector accessors are functions.) <span id="index-VECTOR_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-VECTOR_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fVECTOR_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fVECTOR_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-COMPLEX" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-COMPLEX-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> There are also read-only versions that return a `const` data pointer. For example, the return type of `REAL_RO` is `const double *`. <span id="index-REAL_005fRO" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fRO-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fRO" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fRO-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL_005fRO" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL_005fRO-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW_005fRO" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW_005fRO-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-COMPLEX_005fRO" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-COMPLEX_005fRO-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-STRING_005fPTR_005fRO" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-STRING_005fPTR_005fRO-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-VECTOR_005fPTR_005fRO" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-VECTOR_005fPTR_005fRO-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-DATAPTR_005fRO" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-DATAPTR_005fRO-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> These accessor functions check that they are being used on an appropriate type of `SEXP`. For `VECSXP` and `STRSXP` objects only read-only pointers are available as modifying their data directly would violate assumptions the memory manager depends on. `DATAPTR_RO` returns a generic read-only data pointer for any vector object.

**N.B.** These will return a valid data pointer only for vectors of positive length. Zero-length vectors have no ‘data’ and these accessors will usually return an invalid pointer, for example to address `0x000000000001`. So usages such as

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
memcpy(REAL(newx), REAL_RO(x), LENGTH(x) * sizeof(double));
```

</div>

are undefined behaviour without a prior check on the length of `x`.

Formerly it was possible for packages to obtain internal versions of some accessors by defining ‘`USE_RINTERNALS`’ before including `Rinternals.h`. This is no longer the case. Defining ‘`USE_RINTERNALS`’ now has no effect.

Atomic vector elements can also be accessed and set using element-wise operations like `INTEGER_ELT` and `SET_INTEGER_ELT`. For objects with a compact representation using these may avoid fully materializing the object. In contrast, obtaining a data pointer will have to fully materialize the object. <span id="index-COMPLEX_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-COMPLEX_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fCOMPLEX_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fCOMPLEX_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fINTEGER_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fINTEGER_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fLOGICAL_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fLOGICAL_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fRAW_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fRAW_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fREAL_005fELT" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-SET_005fREAL_005fELT-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Character-encoding-issues" class="section-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Next: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Writing-compact_002drepresentation_002dfriendly-code" rel="next">Writing compact-representation-friendly code</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Vector-accessor-functions" rel="prev">Vector accessor functions</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#System-and-foreign-language-interfaces" rel="up">System and foreign language interfaces</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

### 5.15 Character encoding issues <a href="#Character-encoding-issues-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

<span id="index-Rf_005ftranslateChar" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005ftranslateChar-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005ftranslateCharUTF8" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005ftranslateCharUTF8-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

`CHARSXP`s can be marked as coming from a known encoding (Latin-1 or UTF-8). This is mainly intended for human-readable output, and most packages can just treat such `CHARSXP`s as a whole. However, if they need to be interpreted as characters or output at C level then it would normally be correct to ensure that they are converted to the encoding of the current locale: this can be done by accessing the data in the `CHARSXP` by `Rf_translateChar` rather than by `CHAR`. If re-encoding is needed this allocates memory with `R_alloc` which thus persists to the end of the `.Call`/`.External` call unless `vmaxset` is used (see <a href="#Transient-storage-allocation" class="pxref">Transient storage allocation</a>).

There is a similar function `Rf_translateCharUTF8` which converts to UTF-8: this has the advantage that a faithful translation is almost always possible (whereas only a few languages can be represented in the encoding of the current locale unless that is UTF-8).

Both `Rf_translateChar` and `Rf_translateCharUTF8` will translate any input, using escapes such as ‘`<A9>`’ and ‘`<U+0093>`’ to represent untranslatable parts of the input.

<span id="index-Rf_005fgetCharCE" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fgetCharCE-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fmkCharCE" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fmkCharCE-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

There is a public interface to the encoding marked on `CHARSXPs` *via*

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
typedef enum {CE_NATIVE, CE_UTF8, CE_LATIN1, CE_BYTES, CE_SYMBOL, CE_ANY} cetype_t;
cetype_t Rf_getCharCE(SEXP);
SEXP Rf_mkCharCE(const char *, cetype_t);
```

</div>

Only `CE_UTF8` and `CE_LATIN1` are marked on `CHARSXPs` (and so `Rf_getCharCE` will only return one of the first three), and these should only be used on non-<span class="abbr acronym">ASCII</span> strings. Value `CE_BYTES` is used to make `CHARSXP`s which should be regarded as a set of bytes and not translated. Value `CE_SYMBOL` is used internally to indicate Adobe Symbol encoding. Value `CE_ANY` is used to indicate a character string that will not need re-encoding – this is used for character strings known to be in <span class="abbr acronym">ASCII</span>, and can also be used as an input parameter where the intention is that the string is treated as a series of bytes. (See the comments under `Rf_mkChar` about the length of input allowed.)

Function

<span id="index-Rf_005fcharIsASCII" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcharIsASCII-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
Rboolean Rf_charIsASCII(SEXP);
```

</div>

can be used to detect whether a given `CHARSXP` represents an ASCII string. The implementation is equivalent to checking individual characters, but may be faster.

Function

<span id="index-Rf_005fcharIsUTF8" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcharIsUTF8-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
Rboolean Rf_charIsUTF8(SEXP);
```

</div>

can be used to detect whether the internal representation of a given `CHARSXP` accessed via `CHAR` is UTF-8 (including ASCII). This function is rarely needed and specifically is not needed with `Rf_translateCharUTF8`, because such check is already included. However, when needed, it is better to use it in preference of `Rf_getCharCE`, as it is safer against future changes in the semantics of encoding marks and covers strings internally represented in the native encoding. Note that `Rf_charIsUTF8()` is not equivalent to `getCharCE() == CE_UTF8`.

Similarly, function

<span id="index-Rf_005fcharIsLatin1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fcharIsLatin1-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
Rboolean Rf_charIsLatin1(SEXP);
```

</div>

can be used to detect whether the internal representation of a given `CHARSXP` accessed via `CHAR` is latin1 (including ASCII). It is not equivalent to `Rf_getCharCE() == CE_LATIN1`.

Function

<span id="index-Rf_005freEnc" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005freEnc-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
const char *Rf_reEnc(const char *x, cetype_t ce_in, cetype_t ce_out,
                     int subst);
```

</div>

can be used to re-encode character strings: like `Rf_translateChar` it returns a string allocated by `R_alloc`. This can translate from `CE_SYMBOL` to `CE_UTF8`, but not conversely. Argument `subst` controls what to do with untranslatable characters or invalid input: this is done byte-by-byte with `1` indicates to output hex of the form `<a0>`, and `2` to replace by `.`, with any other value causing the byte to produce no output.

<span id="index-Rf_005fmkCharLenCE" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-Rf_005fmkCharLenCE-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

There is also

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
SEXP Rf_mkCharLenCE(const char *, int, cetype_t);
```

</div>

to create marked character strings of a given length.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

</div>

<div id="Writing-compact_002drepresentation_002dfriendly-code" class="section-level-extent">

<span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Previous: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#Character-encoding-issues" rel="prev">Character encoding issues</a></span></span>, <span class="nav-button"><span class="nav-label">Up: </span><span class="nav-link"><a href="#System-and-foreign-language-interfaces" rel="up">System and foreign language interfaces</a></span></span><span class="nav-button">   </span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#SEC_Contents" rel="contents" title="Table of contents">Contents</a>\]</span><span class="nav-button">\[<a href="#Concept-index" rel="index" title="Index">Index</a>\]</span>

### 5.16 Writing compact-representation-friendly code <a href="#Writing-compact_002drepresentation_002dfriendly-code-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

A simple way to iterate in C over the elements of an atomic vector is to obtain a data pointer and index into that pointer with standard C indexing. However, if the object has a compact representation, then obtaining the data pointer will force the object to be fully materialized. An alternative is to use one of the following functions to query whether a data pointer is available.

<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`const int *` **LOGICAL_OR_NULL** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-LOGICAL_005fOR_005fNULL-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`const int *` **INTEGER_OR_NULL** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-INTEGER_005fOR_005fNULL-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`const double *` **REAL_OR_NULL** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-REAL_005fOR_005fNULL-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`const Rcomplex *` **COMPLEX_OR_NULL** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-COMPLEX_005fOR_005fNULL-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`const Rbyte *` **RAW_OR_NULL** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-RAW_005fOR_005fNULL-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`const void *` **DATAPTR_OR_NULL** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-DATAPTR_005fOR_005fNULL-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
These functions will return a data pointer if one is available. For vectors with a compact representation these functions will return `NULL`.

<span id="index-LOGICAL_005fOR_005fNULL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL_005fOR_005fNULL-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fOR_005fNULL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fOR_005fNULL-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fOR_005fNULL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fOR_005fNULL-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-COMPLEX_005fOR_005fNULL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-COMPLEX_005fOR_005fNULL-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW_005fOR_005fNULL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW_005fOR_005fNULL-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-DATAPTR_005fOR_005fNULL" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-DATAPTR_005fOR_005fNULL-2" class="index-entry-id"></span>

If a data pointer is not available, then code can access elements one at a time with functions like `REAL_ELT`. This is often sufficient, but in some cases can be inefficient. An alternative is to request data for contiguous blocks of elements. For a good choice of block size this can be nearly as efficient as direct pointer access.

<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`R_xlen_t` **INTEGER_GET_REGION** `(SEXP ``sx``, R_xlen_t ``i``, R_xlen_t ``n``, int *``buf``)` <a href="#index-INTEGER_005fGET_005fREGION-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`R_xlen_t` **LOGICAL_GET_REGION** `(SEXP ``sx``, R_xlen_t ``i``, R_xlen_t ``n``, int *``buf``)` <a href="#index-LOGICAL_005fGET_005fREGION-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`R_xlen_t` **REAL_GET_REGION** `(SEXP ``sx``, R_xlen_t ``i``, R_xlen_t ``n``, double *``buf``)` <a href="#index-REAL_005fGET_005fREGION-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`R_xlen_t` **COMPLEX_GET_REGION** `(SEXP ``sx``, R_xlen_t ``i``, R_xlen_t ``n``, Rcomplex *``buf``)` <a href="#index-COMPLEX_005fGET_005fREGION-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`R_xlen_t` **RAW_GET_REGION** `(SEXP ``sx``, R_xlen_t ``i``, R_xlen_t ``n``, Rbyte *``buf``)` <a href="#index-RAW_005fGET_005fREGION-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
These functions copy a contiguous set of up to `n` elements starting with element `i` into a buffer `buf`. The return value is the actual number of elements copied, which may be less than `n`.

<span id="index-INTEGER_005fGET_005fREGION" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fGET_005fREGION-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL_005fGET_005fREGION" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL_005fGET_005fREGION-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fGET_005fREGION" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fGET_005fREGION-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-COMPLEX_005fGET_005fREGION" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-COMPLEX_005fGET_005fREGION-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW_005fGET_005fREGION" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-RAW_005fGET_005fREGION-2" class="index-entry-id"></span>

Macros in `R_ext/Itermacros.h` may help in implementing an iteration strategy.

Some functions useful in implementing new alternate representation (ALTREP) classes, beyond those defined in `R_ext/Altrep.h`, include `ALTREP`, `R_altrep_data1`, `R_set_altrep_data1`, `R_altrep_data2`, `R_set_altrep_data2`, and `DATAPTR_RW`. <span id="index-ALTREP" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-ALTREP-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005faltrep_005fdata1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005faltrep_005fdata1-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fset_005faltrep_005fdata1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fset_005faltrep_005fdata1-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fset_005faltrep_005fdata2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fset_005faltrep_005fdata2-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005faltrep_005fdata2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005faltrep_005fdata2-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-DATAPTR_005fRW" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-DATAPTR_005fRW-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005fext_002fAltrep_002eh" class="index-entry-id"></span> The class of an ALTREP object is identified by a class name symbol and a package name symbol; these can be retrieved using `R_altrep_class_name` and `R_altrep_class_package`, <span id="index-R_005faltrep_005fclass_005fname" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005faltrep_005fclass_005fname-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005faltrep_005fclass_005fpackage" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-R_005faltrep_005fclass_005fpackage-1" class="index-entry-id"></span> The function `ALTREP_CLASS` is also available but is not likely to be needed and may be removed. The type and contents of the value returned by `ALTREP_CLASS` are subject to change. <span id="index-ALTREP_005fCLASS" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-ALTREP_005fCLASS-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

For some objects it may be possible to very efficiently determine whether the object is sorted or contains no `NA` values. These functions can be used to query this information:

<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`int` **LOGICAL_NO_NA** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-LOGICAL_005fNO_005fNA-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`int` **INTEGER_NO_NA** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-INTEGER_005fNO_005fNA-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`int` **REAL_NO_NA** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-REAL_005fNO_005fNA-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`int` **STRING_NO_NA** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-STRING_005fNO_005fNA-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
A `TRUE` result means it is known that there are no `NA` values. A `FALSE` result means it is not known whether there are any `NA` values.

<span id="index-LOGICAL_005fNO_005fNA" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-LOGICAL_005fNO_005fNA-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fNO_005fNA" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fNO_005fNA-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fNO_005fNA" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fNO_005fNA-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-STRING_005fNO_005fNA" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-STRING_005fNO_005fNA-2" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`int` **INTEGER_IS_SORTED** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-INTEGER_005fIS_005fSORTED-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`int` **REAL_IS_SORTED** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-REAL_005fIS_005fSORTED-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>\
<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`int` **STRING_IS_SORTED** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-STRING_005fIS_005fSORTED-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
These functions return one of `SORTED_DECR`, `SORTED_INCR`, or `UNKNOWN_SORTEDNESS`.

<span id="index-INTEGER_005fIS_005fSORTED" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-INTEGER_005fIS_005fSORTED-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fIS_005fSORTED" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-REAL_005fIS_005fSORTED-2" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-STRING_005fIS_005fSORTED" class="index-entry-id"></span> <span id="index-STRING_005fIS_005fSORTED-2" class="index-entry-id"></span>

<span class="category-def">Function: </span>`SEXP` **R_tryWrap** `(SEXP ``x``)` <a href="#index-R_005ftryWrap-1" class="copiable-link">¶</a>  
Try to wrap an object in a wrapper to avoid duplication overhead when changing attributes. Very experimental and might change or be dropped.

## 6 The R <span class="abbr acronym">API</span>: entry points for C code <a href="#The-R-API_003a-entry-points-for-C-code" class="copiable-link">¶</a>

There are a large number of entry points in the R executable/DLL that can be called from C code (and a few that can be called from Fortran code). Only those documented here are stable enough that they will only be changed with considerable notice.

As explained elsewhere in this manual, these functions should only be called from the main thread of the R process. (Doing otherwise can result in memory corruption and very hard-to-debug segfaults.)

The recommended procedure to use these is to include the header file `R.h` in your C code by

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
#include <R.h>
```

</div>

This will include several other header files from the directory `R_INCLUDE_DIR``/R_ext`, and there are other header files there that can be included too, but many of the features they contain should be regarded as undocumented and unstable.

Most of these header files, including all those included by `R.h`, can be used from C++ code. (However, they cannot safely be included in a `extern "C" { }` block as they may include C++ headers when included from C++ code—and whether this succeeds is system-specific).

> **Note:** Because R re-maps many of its external names to avoid clashes with system or user code, it is *essential* to include the appropriate header files when using these entry points.

This remapping can cause problems<a href="#FOOT165" id="DOCF165" class="footnote"><sup>165</sup></a>, and can be eliminated by defining `R_NO_REMAP` (before including any R headers) and prepending ‘`Rf_`’ to *all* the function names used from `Rinternals.h` and `R_ext/Error.h`. These problems can usually be avoided by including other headers (such as system headers and those for external software used by the package) before any R headers. (Headers from other packages may include R headers directly or *via* inclusion from further packages, and may define `R_NO_REMAP` with or without including `Rinternals.h`.) <span id="index-R_005fext_002fError_002eh" class="index-entry-id"></span>

As from R 4.5.0, `R_NO_REMAP` is always defined when the R headers are included from C++ code.

If you decide to define `R_NO_REMAP` in your code, do use something like

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
#ifndef R_NO_REMAP
# define R_NO_REMAP
#endif
```

</div>

to avoid distracting compiler warnings.

Some of these entry points are declared in header `Rmath.h`, most of which are remapped there. That remapping can be eliminated by defining `R_NO_REMAP_RMATH` (before including any R headers) and prepending ‘`Rf_`’ to the function names used from that header except

<div class="example">

``` example-preformatted
exp_rand norm_rand unif_rand signrank_free wilcox_free
```

</div>

We can classify the entry points as

*API*  
Entry points which are documented in this manual and declared in an installed header file. These can be used in distributed packages and ideally will only be changed after deprecation. See <a href="#API-index" class="xref">API index</a>.

*experimental*  
Entry points declared in an installed header file that are part of an experimental API, such as `R_ext/Altrep.h`. These are subject to change, so package authors wishing to use these should be prepared to adapt. See <a href="#Experimental-API-index" class="xref">Experimental API index</a>. <span id="index-R_005fext_002fAltrep_002eh-1" class="index-entry-id"></span>

*embedding*  
Entry points intended primarily for embedding and creating new front-ends. It is not clear that this needs to be a separate category, but it may be useful to keep it separate for now. See <a href="#Embedding-API-index" class="xref">Embedding API index</a>.

*private*  
Entry points that are used when building R and exported on all R platforms but are not declared in the installed header files. Do not use these in distributed code.

*hidden*  
Entry points that are where possible (Windows and some modern Unix-alike compilers/loaders when using R as a shared library) not exported.

As of R 4.6.0 there should no longer be any entry points or variables declared in installed header files that are not part of one of the API groups.

If you would like to use an entry point or variable that is not identified as part of the API in this document, or is currently hidden, you can make a request for it to be made available. Entry points or variables not identified as in the API may be changed or removed with no notice as part of efforts to improve aspects of R.

**Work in progress:** Currently Entry points in the API are identified in the source for this document with `@apifun`, `@eapifun`, and `@embfun` entries. Similarly, `@apivar`, `@eapivar`, and `@embvar` identify variables, and `@apihdr`, `@eapihdr`, and `@embhdr` identify headers in the API. `@forfun` identifies entry points to be called as Fortran subroutines. This could be used for programmatic extraction, but the specific format is work in progress and even the way this document is produced is subject to change.
